entries.83cab8a8bcc8ffbc541105ffa5edfaa46ce63388: <div sID="gen21769" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Matt.8" sID="Matt.8"/> <div eID="gen21769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21770" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> The evangelist having, in the foregoing chapters, given us a specimen of our Lord's preaching, proceeds now to give some instances of the miracles he wrought, which prove him a Teacher come from God, and the great Healer of a diseased world. In this chapter we have, I. Christ's cleansing of a leper, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. His curing a palsy and fever, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.5-Matt.8.18">ver. 5-18</reference>. III. His communing with two that were disposed to follow him, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.19-Matt.8.22">ver. 19-22</reference>. IV. His controlling the tempest, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.23-Matt.8.27">ver. 23-27</reference>. V. His casting out devils, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.28-Matt.8.34">ver. 28-34</reference>.
entries.9817642e9f32a9caa7f8f72dcd0039bc92ff3dc4: <div eID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21770" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Leper Healed.</title> <div sID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When he was come down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him. <hi type="super">2</hi> And, behold, there came a leper and worshipped him, saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Jesus put forth <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jesus saith unto him, See thou tell no man; but go thy way, show thyself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them. <div eID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21773" type="x-p"/> The first verse refers to the close of the foregoing sermon: the people that heard him were <hi type="italic">astonished at his doctrine;</hi> and the effect was, that <hi type="italic">when he came down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him;</hi> though he was so strict a Lawgiver, and so faithful a Reprover, they diligently attended him, and were loth to disperse, and go from him. Note, They to whom Christ has manifested himself, cannot but desire to be better acquainted with him. They who know much of Christ should covet to know more; and <hi type="italic">then shall we know, if we</hi> thus <hi type="italic">follow on to know the Lord.</hi> It is pleasing to see people so well affected to Christ, as to think they can never hear enough of him; so well affected to the best things, as thus to flock after good preaching, and to <hi type="italic">follow the Lamb</hi> withersoever he goes. Now was Jacob's prophecy concerning the Messiah fulfilled, that <hi type="italic">unto him shall the gathering of the people be;</hi> yet they who gathered to him did not cleave to him. They who followed him closely and constantly were but few, compared with the multitudes that were but followers at large. <div eID="gen21773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21774" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">these verses</reference> we have an account of Christ's <hi type="italic">cleansing a leper.</hi> It should seem, by comparing <reference osisRef="Mark.1.40">Mark i. 40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.5.12">and Luke v. 12</reference>, that this passage, though placed, by St. Matthew, after the sermon on the mount, because he would give account of his doctrine first, and then of his miracles, happened some time before; but that is not at all material. This is fitly recorded with the first of Christ's miracles, 1. Because the leprosy was looked upon, among the Jews, as a particular mark of God's displeasure: hence we find Miriam, Gehazi, and Uzziah, smitten with leprosy for some one particular sin; and therefore Christ, to show that he came to turn away the wrath of God, by taking away sin, began with the cure of a leper. 2. Because this disease, as it was supposed to come immediately from the hand of God, so also it was supposed to be removed immediately by his hand, and therefore it was not attempted to be cured by physicians, but was put under the inspection of the priests, the Lord's ministers, who waited to see what God would do. And its being in a garment, or in the walls of a house, was altogether supernatural: and it should seem to be a disease of a quite different nature from what we now call the leprosy. The king of Israel said, <hi type="italic">Am I God,</hi> that I am sent to, to <hi type="italic">recover a man of a leprosy?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.7">2 Kings v. 7</reference>. Christ proved himself God, by recovering many from the leprosy, and authorizing his disciples, in his name, to do so too (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.8">ch. x. 8</reference>), and it is put among the proofs of his being the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">ch. xi. 5</reference>. He also showed himself to be the Saviour of his people from their sins; for though every disease is both the fruit of sin, and a figure of it, as the disorder of the soul, yet the leprosy was in a special manner so; for it contracted such a pollution, and obliged to such a separation from holy things, as no other disease did; and therefore in the laws concerning it (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.14.57">Lev. xiii. and xiv.</reference>), it is treated, not as a sickness, but as an uncleanness; the priest was to pronounce the party clean or unclean, according to the indications: but the honour of making the lepers clean was reserved for Christ, who was to do it as the <hi type="italic">High Priest of our profession;</hi> he comes to do that which the <hi type="italic">law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>. The law discovered sin (for by the law is the knowledge of sin), and pronounced sinners unclean; it shut them up (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.23">Gal. iii. 23</reference>), as the priest did the leper, but could go no further; it could not <hi type="italic">make the comers thereunto perfect.</hi> But Christ takes away sin; cleanses us from it, and so <hi type="italic">perfecteth for ever them that are sanctified.</hi> Now here we have, <div eID="gen21774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21775" type="x-p"/> I. The leper's address to Christ. If this happened, as it is here placed, after the sermon on the mount, we may suppose that the leper, though shut out by his disease from the cities of Israel, yet got within hearing of Christ's sermon, and was encouraged by it to make his application to him; for he that taught <hi type="italic">as one having authority,</hi> could heal so; and therefore he <hi type="italic">came and worshipped him,</hi> as one clothed with a divine power. His address is, <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.</hi> The cleaning of him may be considered, <div eID="gen21775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21776" type="x-p"/> 1. As a temporal mercy; a mercy to the body, delivering it from a disease, which, though it did not threaten life, embittered it. And so it directs us, not only to apply ourselves to Christ, who has power over bodily diseases, for the cure of them, but it also teaches us in what manner to apply ourselves to him; with an assurance of his power, believing that he is as able to cure diseases now, as he was when on earth, but with a submission to his will; <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst.</hi> As to temporal mercies, we cannot be so sure of God's <hi type="italic">will</hi> to bestow them, as we may of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> for his <hi type="italic">power</hi> in them is unlimited by a regard to his glory and our good: when we cannot be sure of his will, we may be sure of his wisdom and mercy, to which we may cheerfully refer ourselves; <hi type="italic">Thy will be done:</hi> and this makes the expectation easy, and the event, when it comes, comfortable. <div eID="gen21776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21777" type="x-p"/> 2. As a typical mercy. Sin is the leprosy of the soul; it shuts us out from communion with God, to which that we maybe restored, it is necessary that we be cleansed from this leprosy, and this ought to be our great concern. Now observe, It is our comfort when we apply ourselves to Christ, as the great Physician, that if he will, he can make us clean; and we should, with an humble, believing boldness, go to him and tell him so. That is, (1.) We must rest ourselves upon his power; we must be confident of this, that Christ <hi type="italic">can</hi> make us clean. No guilt is so great but that there is a sufficiency in his righteousness to atone for it; no corruption so strong, but there is a sufficiency in his grace to subdue it. God would not appoint a physician to his hospital that is not <hi type="italic">par negotio—every way qualified for the undertaking.</hi> (2.) We must recommend ourselves to his pity; we cannot demand it as a debt, but we must humbly request it as a favour; "<hi type="italic">Lord, if thou wilt.</hi> I throw myself at thy feet, and if I perish, I will perish there." <div eID="gen21777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21778" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's answer to this address, which was very kind, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.3">v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen21778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21779" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">He put forth his hand and touched him.</hi> The leprosy was a noisome, loathsome disease, yet Christ touched him; for he did not disdain to converse with publicans and sinners, to do them good. There was a ceremonial pollution contracted by the touch of a leper; but Christ would show, that when he conversed with sinners, he was in no danger of being infected by them, for the prince of this world had nothing in him. If we touch pitch, we are defiled; but Christ was <hi type="italic">separate from sinners,</hi> even when he lived among them. <div eID="gen21779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21780" type="x-p"/> 2. He said, <hi type="italic">I will, be thou clean.</hi> He did not say, as Elisha to Naaman, <hi type="italic">Go, wash in Jordan;</hi> did not put him upon a tedious, troublesome, chargeable course of a physic, but spake the word and healed him. (1.) Here is a word of kindness, <hi type="italic">I will;</hi> I am as willing to help thee, as thou art to be helped. Note, They who by faith apply themselves to Christ for mercy and grace, may be sure that he is willing, freely willing, to give them the mercy and grace they come to him for. Christ is a Physician, that does not need to be sought for, he is always in the way; does not need to be urged, while we are yet speaking, he hears; does not need to be feed, he heals freely, not for price nor reward. He has given all possible demonstration, that he is as willing as he is able to save sinners. (2.) A word of power, <hi type="italic">Be thou clean.</hi> Both a power of authority, and a power of energy, are exerted in this word. Christ heals by a word of command to us; <hi type="italic">Be thou clean;</hi> "Be willing to be clean, and use the means; cleanse thyself from all filthiness;" but there goes along with this a word of command concerning us, a word that does the work; <hi type="italic">I will that thou be clean.</hi> Such a word as this is necessary to the cure, and effectual for it; and the Almighty grace which speaks it, shall not be wanting to those who truly desire it. <div eID="gen21780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21781" type="x-p"/> III. The happy change hereby wrought: <hi type="italic">Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.</hi> Nature works gradually, but the God of nature works immediately; he speaks it, it is done; and yet he works effectually; he <hi type="italic">commands, and it stands fast.</hi> One of the first miracles Moses wrought, was curing himself of a leprosy (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.7">Exod. iv. 7</reference>), for the priests under the law offered sacrifices first for their own sin; but one of Christ's first miracles was curing another of leprosy, for he had no sin of his own to atone for. <div eID="gen21781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21782" type="x-p"/> IV. The after-directions Christ gave him. It is fit that they who are cured by Christ should ever after be ruled by him. <div eID="gen21782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21783" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">See thou tell no man;</hi> "Tell no man till thou has shown thyself to the priest, and he has pronounced thee clean; and so thou hast a legal proof, both that thou wast before a leper, and art now thoroughly cleansed." Christ would have his miracles to appear in their full light and evidence, and not to be published till they could appear so. Note, They that preach the truths of Christ should be able to prove them; to defend what they preach, and <hi type="italic">convince gainsayers. "Tell no man, till thou hast showed thyself to the priest,</hi> lest if he hear who cured thee, he should out of spite deny to give thee a certificate of the cure, and so keep thee under confinement." Such were the priests in Christ's time, that they who had any thing to do with them had need to have been as wise as serpents. <div eID="gen21783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21784" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Go show thyself to the priest,</hi> according to the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.2">Lev. xiv. 2</reference>. Christ took care to have the law observed, lest he should give offence, and to show that he will have order kept up, and good discipline and respect paid to those that are in office. It may be of use to those that are cleansed of their spiritual leprosy, to have recourse to Christ's ministers, and to open their case to them, that they may assist them in their enquiries into their spiritual state, and advise, and comfort, and pray for them. <div eID="gen21784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21785" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Offer the gift that Moses commanded,</hi> in token of thankfulness to God, and recompence to the priest for his pains; and this <hi type="italic">for a testimony unto them;</hi> either, (1.) Which <hi type="italic">Moses commanded for a testimony:</hi> the ceremonial laws were testimonies of God's authority over them, care of them, and of that grace which should afterwards be revealed. Or, (2.) "Do thou offer it for a testimony, and let the priest know who cleansed thee, and how; and it shall be a testimony, that there is one among them who does that which the high priest cannot do. Let it remain upon record as a witness of my power, and a testimony for me <hi type="italic">to</hi> them, if they will use it and improve it; but <hi type="italic">against</hi> them, if they will not:" for so Christ's word and works are testimonies.
entries.89a0d02af8dcd57f1f7fb5f398f2cfd5fcb36fce: <div eID="gen21785" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Heals the Centurion's Servant.</title> <div sID="gen21786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And when Jesus was entered into Capernaum, there came unto him a centurion, beseeching him, <hi type="super">6</hi> And saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Jesus saith unto him, I will come and heal him. <hi type="super">8</hi> The centurion answered and said, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed. <hi type="super">9</hi> For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this <hi type="italic">man,</hi> Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> When Jesus heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. <hi type="super">12</hi> But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Jesus said unto the centurion, Go thy way; and as thou hast believed, <hi type="italic">so</hi> be it done unto thee. And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour. <div eID="gen21786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21787" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's curing the centurion's servant of a palsy. This was done at Capernaum, where Christ now dwelt, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">ch. iv. 13</reference>. Christ went about doing good, and came home to do good too; every place he came to was the better for him. <div eID="gen21787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21788" type="x-p"/> The persons Christ had now to do with were, <div eID="gen21788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21789" type="x-p"/> 1. A <hi type="italic">centurion;</hi> he was a supplicant, a Gentile, a Roman, an officer of the army; probably commander-in-chief of that part of the Roman army which was quartered at Capernaum, and kept garrison there. (1.) Though he was a soldier (and a little piety commonly goes a great way with men of that profession), yet he was a godly man; he was eminently so. Note, God has his remnant among all sorts of people. No man's calling or place in the world will be an excuse for his unbelief and impiety; none shall say in the great day, I had been religious, if I had not been a soldier; for such there are among the <hi type="italic">ransomed of the Lord.</hi> And sometimes where grace conquers the unlikely, it is more than a conqueror; this soldier that was good, was very good. (2.) Though he was a Roman soldier, and his very dwelling among the Jews was a badge of their subjection to the Roman yoke, yet Christ, who was <hi type="italic">King of the Jews,</hi> favoured him; and therein has taught us to do good to our enemies, and not needlessly to interest ourselves in national enmities. (3.) Though he was a Gentile, yet Christ countenanced him. It is true, he went not to any of the Gentile towns (it was the land of Canaan that was Immanuel's land, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Isa. viii. 8</reference>), yet he received addresses from Gentiles; now good old Simeon's word began to be fulfilled, that he should be <hi type="italic">a light to lighten the Gentiles,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">the glory of his people Israel.</hi> Matthew, in annexing this cure to that of the leper, who was a Jew, intimates this; the leprous Jews Christ touched and cured, for he preached personally to them; but the paralytic Gentiles he cured at a distance; for to them he did not go in person, but <hi type="italic">sent his word and healed them;</hi> yet in them he was more magnified. <div eID="gen21789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21790" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The centurion's servant;</hi> he was the patient. In this also it appears, that there is no respect of persons with God; for <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus,</hi> as there is <hi type="italic">neither circumcision nor uncircumcision,</hi> so there is <hi type="italic">neither bond nor free.</hi> He is as ready to heal the poorest servant, as the richest master; for himself <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant,</hi> to show his regard to the meanest. <div eID="gen21790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21791" type="x-p"/> Now in the story of the cure of this servant, we may observe an intercourse or interchanging of graces, very remarkable between Christ and the centurion. See here, <div eID="gen21791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21792" type="x-p"/> I. The grace of the centurion working towards Christ. Can any good thing come out of a Roman soldier? any thing tolerable, much less any thing laudable? Come and see, and you will find abundance of good coming out of this centurion that was eminent and exemplary. Observe, 1. His affectionate address to Jesus Christ, which speaks, <div eID="gen21792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21793" type="x-p"/> (1.) A pious regard to our great Master, as one able and willing to succour and relieve poor petitioners. He came to him <hi type="italic">beseeching him,</hi> not as Naaman the Syrian (a centurion too) came to Elisha, demanding a cure, taking state, and standing upon points of honour; but with cap in hand as a humble suitor. By this it seems that he saw more in Christ than appeared at first view; saw that which commanded respect, though to those who looked no further, his visage was marred more than any man's. The officers of the army, being comptrollers of the town, no doubt made a great figure, yet he lays by the thoughts of his post of honour, when he addresses himself to Christ, and comes <hi type="italic">beseeching him.</hi> Note, the greatest of men must turn beggars, when they have to do with Christ. He owns Christ's sovereignty, in calling him Lord, and referring the case to him, and to his will, and wisdom, by a modest remonstrance, without any formal and express petition. He knew he had to do with a wise and gracious Physician, to whom the opening of the malady was equivalent to the most earnest request. A humble confession of our spiritual wants and diseases shall not fail of an answer of peace. Pour out thy complaint, and mercy shall be poured out. <div eID="gen21793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21794" type="x-p"/> (2.) A charitable regard to his poor servant. We read of many that came to Christ for their children, but this is the only instance of one that came to him for a servant: <hi type="italic">Lord, my servant lieth at home sick.</hi> Note, it is the duty of masters to concern themselves for their servants, when they are in affliction. The palsy disabled the servant for his work, and made him as troublesome and tedious as any distemper could, yet he did not turn him away when he was sick (as that Amalekite did his servants, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.13">1 Sam. xxx. 13</reference>), did not send him to his friends, not let him lie by neglected, but sought out the best relief he could for him; the servant could not have done more for the master, than the master did here for the servant. The centurion's servants were very dutiful to him (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.9">v. 9</reference>), and here we see what made them so; he was very kind to them, and that made them the more cheerfully obedient to him. As we must not despise the <hi type="italic">cause of our servants, when they contend with us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.13">Job xxxi. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">15</reference>), so we must not despise their case when God contends with them; for we are made in the same mould, by the same hand, and stand upon the same level with them before God, and must not set them <hi type="italic">with the dogs of our flock.</hi> The centurion applies not to witches or wizards for his servant, but to Christ. The palsy is a disease in which the physician's skill commonly fails; it was therefore a great evidence of his faith in the power of Christ, to come to him for a cure, which was above the power of natural means to effect. Observe, How pathetically he represents his servant's case as very sad; he is <hi type="italic">sick of the palsy,</hi> a disease which commonly makes the patient senseless of pain, but this person was <hi type="italic">grievously tormented;</hi> being young, nature was strong to struggle with the stroke, which made it painful. (It was not <hi type="italic">paralysis simplex,</hi> but <hi type="italic">scorbutica</hi>). We should thus concern ourselves for the souls of our children, and servants, that are spiritually sick of the palsy, the dead-palsy, the dumb palsy; senseless of spiritual evils, inactive in that which is spiritually good, and bring them to the means of healing and health. <div eID="gen21794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21795" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe his great humility and self-abasement. After Christ had intimated his readiness to come and heal his servants (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.7">v. 7</reference>), he expressed himself with the more humbleness of mind. Note, Humble souls are made more humble, by Christ's gracious condescensions to them. Observe what was the language of his humility; <hi type="italic">Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.8">v. 8</reference>), which speaks mean thought of himself, and high thoughts of our Lord Jesus. He does not say, "My servant is not worthy that thou shouldest come into his chamber, because it is in the garret;" But <hi type="italic">I am not worthy that thou shouldest come into my house.</hi> The centurion was a great man, yet he owned his unworthiness before God. Note, Humility very well becomes persons of quality. Christ now made but a mean figure in the world, yet the centurion, looking upon him as a prophet, <hi type="italic">yea, more than a prophet,</hi> paid him this respect. Note, We should have a value and veneration for what we see of God, even in those who, in outward condition, are every way our inferiors. The centurion came to Christ with a petition, and therefore expressed himself thus humbly. Note, In all our approaches to Christ, and to God through Christ, it becomes us to abase ourselves, and to lie low in the sense of our own unworthiness, as mean creatures and as vile sinners, to do any thing for God, to receive any good from him, or to have any thing to do with him. <div eID="gen21795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21796" type="x-p"/> 3. Observe his great faith. The more humility the more faith; the more diffident we are of ourselves, the stronger will be our confidence in Jesus Christ. He had an assurance of faith not only that Christ could cure his servant, but, <div eID="gen21796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21797" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he could cure him at a distance. There needed not any physical contact, as in natural operations, nor any application to the part affected; but the cure, he believed, might be wrought, without bringing the physician and patient together. We read afterwards of those, who brought the <hi type="italic">man sick of the palsy to Christ,</hi> through much difficulty, and set him before him; and Christ commended their faith for a <hi type="italic">working</hi> faith. This centurion did not bring his man <hi type="italic">sick of the palsy,</hi> and Christ commended his faith for a <hi type="italic">trusting</hi> faith: true faith is accepted of Christ, though variously appearing: Christ puts the best construction upon the different methods of religion that people take, and thereby has taught us to do so too. This centurion believed, and it is undoubtedly true, that the power of Christ knows no limits, and therefore nearness and distance are alike to him. Distance of place cannot obstruct either the knowing or working of him that <hi type="italic">fills all places. Am I a God at hand, says the Lord, and not a God afar off?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.23">Jer. xxiii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen21797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21798" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he could cure him with a <hi type="italic">word,</hi> not send him a medicine, much less a charm; but <hi type="italic">speak the word only,</hi> and I do not question but <hi type="italic">my servant shall be healed.</hi> Herein he owns him to have a divine power, an authority to command all the creatures and powers of nature, which enables him to do whatsoever he pleases in the kingdom of nature; as at first he raised that kingdom by an almighty word, when he said, <hi type="italic">Let there be light.</hi> With men, saying and doing are two things; but not so with Christ, who is therefore the <hi type="italic">Arm of the Lord,</hi> because he is the <hi type="italic">eternal Word.</hi> His saying, <hi type="italic">Be ye warmed and filled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 16</reference>), and healed, warms, and fills and heals. <div eID="gen21798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21799" type="x-p"/> The centurion's faith in the power of Christ he here illustrates by the dominion he had, as a centurion, over his soldiers, as a master over his servants; he says to one, <hi type="italic">Go, and he goes, &c.</hi> They were all at his beck and command, so as that he could by them execute things at a distance; his word was a law to them—<hi type="italic">dictum factum;</hi> well-disciplined soldiers know that the commands of their officers are not to be disputed, but obeyed. Thus could Christ speak, and it is done; such a power had he over all bodily diseases. The centurion had this command over his soldiers, though he was himself a <hi type="italic">man under authority;</hi> not a commander-in-chief, but a subaltern officer; much more had Christ this power, who is the supreme and sovereign Lord of all. The centurion's servants were very obsequious, would go and come at every the least intimation of their master's mind. Now, [1.] Such servants we all should be to God: we must go and come at his bidding, according to the directions of his word, and the disposals of his providence; run where he sends us, return when he remands us, and do what he appoints. <hi type="italic">What saith my Lord unto his servant?</hi> When his will crosses our own, his must take place, and our own be set aside. [2.] Such servants bodily diseases are to Christ. They seize us when he sends them; they leave us when he calls them back; they have that effect upon us, upon our bodies, upon our souls, that he orders. It is a matter of comfort to all that belong to Christ, for whose good his power is exerted and engaged, that every disease has his commission, executes his command, is under his control, and is made to serve the intentions of his grace. They need not fear sickness, nor what it can do, who see it in the hand of so good a Friend. <div eID="gen21799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21800" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the grace of Christ appearing towards this centurion; for to the gracious he will show himself gracious. <div eID="gen21800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21801" type="x-p"/> 1. He complies with his address at the first word. He did but tell him his servant's case, and was going on to beg a cure, when Christ prevented him, with this good word, and comfortable word, <hi type="italic">I will come and heal him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.7">v. 7</reference>); not <hi type="italic">I will come and see him</hi>—that had evinced him a kind Saviour; but, <hi type="italic">I will come and heal him</hi>—that shows him a mighty, an almighty Saviour; it was a great word, but no more than he could make good; for he has <hi type="italic">healing under his wings;</hi> his coming is healing. They who wrought miracles by a derived power, did not speak thus positively, as Christ did, who wrought them by his own power, as one that had authority. When a minister is sent for to a sick friend, he can but say, <hi type="italic">I will come and pray for him;</hi> but Christ says, <hi type="italic">I will come and heal him:</hi> it is well that Christ can do more for us than our ministers can. The centurion desired he would heal his servant; he says, <hi type="italic">I will come and heal him;</hi> thus expressing more favour than he did either ask or think of. Note, Christ often outdoes the expectations of poor supplicants. See an instance of Christ's humility, that he would make a visit to a poor soldier. He would not go down to see a nobleman's sick child, who insisted upon his coming down (<reference osisRef="John.4.47-John.4.49">John iv. 47-49</reference>), but he proffers to go down to see a sick servant; thus does he regard <hi type="italic">the low estate</hi> of his people, and give <hi type="italic">more abundant honour to that part which lacked.</hi> Christ's humility, in being willing to come, gave an example to him, and occasioned his humility, in owning himself unworthy to have him come. Note, Christ's gracious condescensions to us, should make us the more humble and self-abasing before him. <div eID="gen21801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21802" type="x-p"/> 2. He commends his faith, and takes occasion from it to speak a kind word of the poor Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.10-Matt.8.12">v. 10-12</reference>. See what great things a strong but self-denying faith can obtain from Jesus Christ, even of general and public concern. <div eID="gen21802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21803" type="x-p"/> (1.) As to the centurion himself; he not only approved him and accepted him (that honour have all true believers), but he admired him and applauded him: that honour great believers have, as Job; there is <hi type="italic">none like unto him in the earth.</hi> <div eID="gen21803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21804" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ admired him, not for his greatness, but for his graces. <hi type="italic">When Jesus heard it, he marvelled;</hi> not as if it were to him new and surprising, he knew the centurion's faith, for he wrought it; but it was great and excellent, rare and uncommon, and Christ spoke of it as wonderful, to teach us what to admire; not worldly pomp and decorations, but the beauty of holiness, and the ornaments which are <hi type="italic">in the sight of God of great price.</hi> Note, The wonders of grace should affect us more than the wonders of nature or providence, and spiritual attainments more than any achievements in this world. Of those that are <hi type="italic">rich in faith,</hi> not of those that are <hi type="italic">rich in gold and silver,</hi> we should say that they have <hi type="italic">gotten all this glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Gen. xxx. 1</reference>. But whatever there is admirable in the faith of any, it must redound to the glory of Christ, who will shortly be himself <hi type="italic">admired in all them that believe,</hi> as having done in and for them <hi type="italic">marvellous things.</hi> <div eID="gen21804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21805" type="x-p"/> [2.] He <hi type="italic">applauded</hi> him in what he said to <hi type="italic">them that followed.</hi> All believers shall be, <hi type="italic">in the other world,</hi> but some believers are, <hi type="italic">in this world,</hi> confessed and acknowledged by Christ before men, in his eminent appearances for them and with them. <hi type="italic">Verily, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.</hi> Now this speaks, <hi type="italic">First, Honour to the centurion;</hi> who, though not a son of Abraham's loins, was an heir of Abraham's faith, and Christ found it so. Note, The thing that Christ seeks is <hi type="italic">faith,</hi> and wherever it is, he finds it, though but <hi type="italic">as a grain of mustard-seed.</hi> He had not found <hi type="italic">so great faith,</hi> all things considered, and in proportion to the means; as the poor widow is said to <hi type="italic">cast in more than they all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.3">Luke xxi. 3</reference>. Though the centurion was a Gentile, yet he was thus commended. Note, We must be so far from grudging, that we must be forward, to give those their due praise, that are not within our denomination or pale. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It speaks <hi type="italic">shame to Israel,</hi> to whom pertained <hi type="italic">the adoption, the glory, the covenants,</hi> and all the assistances and encouragements of faith. Note, When <hi type="italic">the Son of man comes,</hi> he <hi type="italic">finds</hi> little <hi type="italic">faith,</hi> and, therefore, he finds so little <hi type="italic">fruit.</hi> Note, the attainments of some, who have had but little helps for their souls, will aggravate the sin and ruin of many, that have had great plenty of the means of grace, and have not made a good improvement of them. Christ said this <hi type="italic">to those that followed</hi> him, if by any means he might provoke them to a holy emulation, as Paul speaks, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>. They were Abraham's seed; in jealousy for that honour, let them not suffer themselves to be outstripped by a Gentile, especially in that grace for which Abraham was eminent. <div eID="gen21805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21806" type="x-p"/> (2.) As to others. Christ takes occasion from hence to make a comparison between Jews and Gentiles, and tells them two things, which could not but be very surprising to them who had been taught that <hi type="italic">salvation was of the Jews.</hi> <div eID="gen21806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21807" type="x-p"/> [1.] That <hi type="italic">a great many of the Gentiles should be saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">v. 11</reference>. The faith of the centurion was but a specimen of the conversion of the Gentiles, and a preface to their adoption into the church. This was a topic our Lord Jesus touched often upon; he speaks it with assurance; <hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> "I that know all men;" and he could not say any thing more pleasing to himself, or more displeasing to the Jews; an intimation of this kind enraged the Nazarenes against him, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.27">Luke iv. 27</reference>. Christ gives us here an <hi type="italic">idea, First,</hi> of the <hi type="italic">persons</hi> that shall be <hi type="italic">saved;</hi> many <hi type="italic">from the east and the west:</hi> he had said (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.14">ch. vii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Few there be that find the way of life;</hi> and yet here <hi type="italic">many shall come.</hi> Few at one time, and in one place; yet, when they come altogether, they will be a great many. We now see but here and there one brought to grace; but we shall shortly see the Captain of our salvation <hi type="italic">bringing many sons to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. He will come with <hi type="italic">ten thousands of his saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>), with such a company as <hi type="italic">no man can number</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">with nations of them that are saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.24">Rev. xxi. 24</reference>. They shall come <hi type="italic">from the east</hi> and <hi type="italic">from the west;</hi> places far distant from each other; and yet they shall all meet at the right hand of Christ, the Centre of their unity. Note, God has his remnant in all places; <hi type="italic">from the rising of the sun, to the going down of the same,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>. The elect will be gathered from the four winds, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">ch. xxiv. 31</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">sown in the earth,</hi> some scattered in every corner of the field. The Gentile world lay <hi type="italic">from east to west,</hi> and they are especially meant here; though they were <hi type="italic">strangers to the covenant of promise</hi> now, and had been long, yet who knows what <hi type="italic">hidden ones</hi> God had among them then? As in Elijah's time in Israel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.14">1 Kings xix. 14</reference>), soon after which they flocked into the church in great multitudes, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3-Isa.60.4">Isa. lx. 3, 4</reference>. Note, When we come to heaven, as we shall miss a great many there, that we thought had been going thither, so we shall meet a great many there, that we did not expect. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ gives us an idea of the <hi type="italic">salvation itself.</hi> They shall come, shall come together, shall come together to Christ, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2 Thess. ii. 1</reference>. 1. They shall be admitted <hi type="italic">into the kingdom of grace</hi> on earth, into the covenant of grace made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; they shall be <hi type="italic">blessed with faithful Abraham,</hi> whose blessing comes upon the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal. iii. 14</reference>. This makes Zaccheus a son of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.9">Luke xix. 9</reference>. 2. They shall be admitted into the <hi type="italic">kingdom of glory in heaven.</hi> They shall come cheerfully, flying <hi type="italic">as doves to their windows;</hi> they shall sit down to rest from their labours, as having done their day's work; sitting denotes <hi type="italic">continuance:</hi> while we <hi type="italic">stand,</hi> we are <hi type="italic">going;</hi> where we <hi type="italic">sit,</hi> we mean to <hi type="italic">stay;</hi> heaven is a <hi type="italic">remaining</hi> rest, it is a <hi type="italic">continuing</hi> city; they shall <hi type="italic">sit down,</hi> as upon a throne (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>); as <hi type="italic">at a table;</hi> that is the metaphor here; they shall sit down to be <hi type="italic">feasted;</hi> which denotes both <hi type="italic">fulness</hi> of <hi type="italic">communication,</hi> and <hi type="italic">freedom</hi> and familiarity of communion, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Luke xxii. 30</reference>. They shall <hi type="italic">sit down with Abraham.</hi> They who in this world were ever so far distant from each other in time, place, or outward condition, shall all meet together in heaven; ancients and moderns, Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor. The rich man in hell <hi type="italic">sees</hi> Abraham, but Lazarus <hi type="italic">sits down with him,</hi> leaning on his breast. Note, Holy society is a part of the felicity of heaven; and they on whom the ends of the world are come, and who are most obscure, shall share in glory with the renowned patriarchs. <div eID="gen21807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21808" type="x-p"/> [2.] That a great many of the Jews should perish, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">v. 12</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen21808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21809" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A strange sentence passed; <hi type="italic">The children of the kingdom shall be cast out;</hi> the Jews that persist in unbelief, though they were by birth <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom,</hi> yet shall be cut off from being members of the visible church: <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God,</hi> of which they boasted that they were <hi type="italic">the children,</hi> shall be taken from them, and they shall become <hi type="italic">not a people,</hi> not <hi type="italic">obtaining mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">Rom. xi. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.31">ix. 31</reference>. In the great day it will not avail men to have been <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom,</hi> either as Jews or as Christians; for men will then be judged, not by what they were <hi type="italic">called,</hi> but by what they <hi type="italic">were. If children</hi> indeed, <hi type="italic">then heirs;</hi> but many are children in profession, in the family, but not of it, that will come short of the inheritance. Being born of professing parents denominates us <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom;</hi> but if we rest in that, and have nothing else to show for heaven but that, we shall be <hi type="italic">cast out.</hi> <div eID="gen21809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A strange punishment for <hi type="italic">the workers of iniquity</hi> described; <hi type="italic">They shall be cast into outer darkness,</hi> the darkness of those that are without, of the Gentiles that were out of the church; into that the Jews were cast, and into worse; they were blinded, and hardened, and filled with terrors, as the apostle shows, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8-Rom.11.10">Rom. xi. 8-10</reference>. A people so unchurched and given up to spiritual judgments, are in <hi type="italic">utter darkness</hi> already: but it looks further, to the state of damned sinners in hell, to which the other is a dismal preface. <hi type="italic">They shall be cast out</hi> from God, and all true comfort, and <hi type="italic">cast into darkness.</hi> In hell there is fire, but no light; it is <hi type="italic">utter darkness;</hi> darkness in extremity; the highest degree of darkness, without any remainder, or mixture, or hope, of light; not the least gleam or glimpse of it; it is darkness that results from their being shut out of heaven, the land of light; they who are <hi type="italic">without,</hi> are in <hi type="italic">the regions of darkness;</hi> yet that is not the worst of it, <hi type="italic">there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.</hi> 1. In hell there will be great grief, floods of tears shed to no purpose; anguish of spirit preying eternally upon the vitals, in the sense of the wrath of God, is the torment of the damned. 2. Great indignation: damned sinners will <hi type="italic">gnash their teeth</hi> for spite and vexation, <hi type="italic">full of the fury of the Lord;</hi> seeing with envy the happiness of others, and reflecting with horror upon the former possibility of their own being happy, which is now past. <div eID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21811" type="x-p"/> 3. He cures his servant. He not only commends his application to him, but grants him that for which he applied, which was a real answer, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.13">v. 13</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen21811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21812" type="x-p"/> (1.) What Christ said to him: he said that which made the cure as great a favour to him as it was to his servant, and much greater; <hi type="italic">As thou hast believed, so be it done to thee.</hi> The servant got a cure of his disease, but the master got the confirmation and approbation of his faith. Note, Christ often gives encouraging answers to his praying people, when they are interceding for others. It is kindness to us, to be heard for others. God turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends, <reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job xlii. 10</reference>. It was a great honour which Christ put upon this centurion, when he gave him a blank, as it were; <hi type="italic">Be it done as thou believest.</hi> What could he have more? Yet what was said to him is said to us all, <hi type="italic">Believe, and ye shall receive; only believe.</hi> See here the power of Christ, and the power of faith. As Christ can <hi type="italic">do</hi> what he will, so an active believer may <hi type="italic">have</hi> what he will from Christ; the oil of grace multiplies, and stays not till the vessels of faith fail. <div eID="gen21812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21813" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was the effect of this saying: the prayer of faith was a prevailing prayer, it ever was so, and ever will be so; it appears, by the suddenness of the cure, that it was <hi type="italic">miraculous:</hi> and by its coincidence with Christ's saying, that the miracle was <hi type="italic">his; he spake, and it was done;</hi> and this was a proof of his omnipotence, that he has a long arm. It is the observation of a learned physician, that the diseases Christ cured were chiefly such as were the most difficult to be cured by any natural means, and particularly the palsy. <hi type="italic">Omnis paralysis, præsertim vetusta, aut incurabilis est, aut difficilis curatu, etiam pueris: atque soleo ego dicere, morbos omnes qui Christo curandi fuerunt propositi, difficillimos sua matura curatu esse—Every kind of palsy, especially of long continuance, is either incurable, or is found to yield with the utmost difficulty to medical skill, even in young subjects; so that I have frequently remarked, that all the diseases which were referred to Christ for cure appear to have been of the most obstinate and hopeless kind.</hi> Mercurialis <hi type="italic">De Morbis Puerorum,</hi> lib. 2. cap. 5.
entries.16c3992b36e227db0fa8277e34f221631205fd25: <div eID="gen21813" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Wife's Mother Healed.</title> <div sID="gen21814" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And when Jesus was come into Peter's house, he saw his wife's mother laid, and sick of a fever. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them. <hi type="super">16</hi> When the even was come, they brought unto him many that were possessed with devils: and he cast out the spirits with <hi type="italic">his</hi> word, and healed all that were sick: <hi type="super">17</hi> That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare <hi type="italic">our</hi> sicknesses. <div eID="gen21814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21815" type="x-p"/> They who pretend to be critical in the Harmony of the evangelists, place this passage, and all that follows to the end of <reference osisRef="Matt.8.14-Matt.9.38">ch. ix.</reference> before the sermon on the mount, according to the order which Mark and Luke observe in placing it. Dr. Lightfoot places only this passage before the sermon on the mount, and <reference osisRef="Matt.8.18">v. 18</reference>, &c. after. Here we have, <div eID="gen21815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21816" type="x-p"/> I. A particular account of the cure of <hi type="italic">Peter's wife's mother,</hi> who was ill <hi type="italic">of a fever;</hi> in which observe, <div eID="gen21816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21817" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">case,</hi> which was nothing extraordinary; fevers are the most common distempers; but, the patient being a near relation of Peter's, it is recorded as an instance of Christ's peculiar care of, and kindness to, the families of his disciples. Here we find, (1.) That Peter had a <hi type="italic">wife,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">was called to be an apostle of Christ;</hi> and Christ countenanced the marriage state, by being thus kind to his <hi type="italic">wife's</hi> relations. The church of Rome, therefore, which forbids ministers to marry, goes contrary to that apostle from whom they pretend to derive an infallibility. (2.) That Peter had a <hi type="italic">house,</hi> though Christ had not, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">v. 20</reference>. Thus was the disciple better provided for than his Lord. (3.) That he had a house at Capernaum, though he was originally of Bethsaida; it is probably, he removed to Capernaum, when Christ removed thither, and made that his principal residence. Note, It is worth while to change our quarters, that we may be near to Christ, and have opportunities of converse with him. When the ark removes, Israel must remove and go after it. (4.) That he had his <hi type="italic">wife's mother</hi> with him in his family, which is an example to yoke-fellows to be kind to one another's relations as their own. Probably, this good woman was old, and yet was respected and taken care of, as old people ought to be, with all possible tenderness. (5.) That she lay ill <hi type="italic">of a fever.</hi> Neither the strength of youth, nor the weakness and coldness of age, will be a fence against diseases of this kind. The palsy was a chronical disease, the fever an acute disease, but both were brought to Christ. <div eID="gen21817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21818" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">cure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) How it was <hi type="italic">effected; He touched her hand;</hi> not to know the disease, as the physicians do, by the pulse, but to heal it. This was an intimation of his kindness and tenderness; he is <hi type="italic">himself touched with the feeling of our infirmities;</hi> it likewise shows the way of spiritual healing, by the exerting of the power of Christ with his word, and the application of Christ to ourselves. The scripture <hi type="italic">speaks the word,</hi> the Spirit gives the touch, touches the heart, touches the hand. (2.) How it was <hi type="italic">evidenced:</hi> this showed that the <hi type="italic">fever left her, she arose, and ministered to them.</hi> By this it appears, [1.] That the mercy was perfected. They that recover from fevers by the power of nature are commonly weak and feeble, and unfit for business a great while after; to show therefore that this cure was above the power of nature, she was immediately so well as to go about the business of the house. [2.] That the mercy was sanctified; and the mercies that are so are indeed perfected. Though she was thus dignified by a peculiar favour, yet she does not assume importance, but is as ready to wait at table, if there be occasion, as any servant. They must be humble whom Christ has honoured; being thus delivered, she studies what she shall render. It is very fit that they whom Christ hath healed should minister unto him, as his humble servants, all their days. <div eID="gen21818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21819" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a general account of the many cures that Christ wrought. This cure of Peter's mother-in-law brought him abundance of patients. "He healed such a one; why not me? Such a one's friend, why not mine?" Now we are here told, <div eID="gen21819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21820" type="x-p"/> 1. What he did, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.16">v. 16</reference>. (1.) <hi type="italic">He cast out devils; cast out the</hi> evil <hi type="italic">spirits with his word.</hi> There may be much of Satan's agency, by the divine permission, in those diseases of which natural causes may be assigned, as in Job's boils, especially in the diseases of the mind; but, about the time of Christ's being in the world, there seems to have been more than ordinary letting loose of the devil, to possess and vex the bodies of people; he came, <hi type="italic">having great wrath, for he knew that his time was short;</hi> and God wisely ordered it so, that Christ might have the fairer and more frequent opportunities of showing his power over Satan, and the purpose and design of his coming into the world, which was to disarm and dispossess Satan, to break his power, and to destroy his works; and his success was as glorious as his design was gracious. (2.) <hi type="italic">He healed all that were sick;</hi> all without exception, though the patient was ever so mean, and the case ever so bad. <div eID="gen21820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21821" type="x-p"/> 2. How the scripture was herein fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">v. 17</reference>. The accomplishment of the Old-Testament prophecies was the great thing Christ had in his eye, and the great proof of his being the Messiah: among other things, it was written of him (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa. liii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows:</hi> it is referred to, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1 Pet. ii. 24</reference>, and there it is construed, <hi type="italic">he hath borne our sins;</hi> here it is referred to, and is construed, <hi type="italic">he hath borne our sicknesses;</hi> our sins make our sicknesses our griefs; Christ bore away sin by the merit of his death, and bore away sickness by the miracles of his life; nay, though those miracles are ceased, we may say, that <hi type="italic">he bore our sicknesses</hi> then, <hi type="italic">when he bore our sins in his own body upon the tree;</hi> for sin is both the cause and the sting of sickness. Many are the diseases and calamities to which we are liable in the body: and there is more, in this one line of the gospels, to support and comfort us under them, than in all the writings of the philosophers—that Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">bore our sicknesses, and carried our sorrows;</hi> he bore them before us; though he was never sick, yet he was hungry, and thirsty, and weary, and troubled in spirit, sorrowful and very heavy; he bore them for us in his <hi type="italic">passion,</hi> and bears them with us in <hi type="italic">compassion,</hi> being <hi type="italic">touched with the feeling of our infirmities:</hi> and thus he bears them off from us, and makes them sit light, if it be not our own fault. Observe how emphatically it is expressed here: <hi type="italic">Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses;</hi> he was both able and willing to interpose in that matter, and concerned to deal with <hi type="italic">our infirmities and sicknesses,</hi> as our Physician; that part of the calamity of the human nature was his particular care, which he evidenced by his great readiness to cure diseases; and he is no less powerful, no less tender now, for we are sure that never were any the worse for going to heaven.
entries.6e0bf61fc7a8dbc52419bc32d4d7222c81d05caa: <div eID="gen21821" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Answer to a Scribe and Another.</title> <div sID="gen21822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Now when Jesus saw great multitudes about him, he gave commandment to depart unto the other side. <hi type="super">19</hi> And a certain scribe came, and said unto him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air <hi type="italic">have</hi> nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay <hi type="italic">his</hi> head. <hi type="super">21</hi> And another of his disciples said unto him, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. <hi type="super">22</hi> But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead. <div eID="gen21822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21823" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Christ's removing to <hi type="italic">the other side of the sea of Tiberias,</hi> and his ordering his disciples, whose boats attended him, to get their transport-vessels ready, in order to it, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.18">v. 18</reference>. The influences of this Sun of righteousness were not to be confined to one place, but diffused all the country over; he must go about to do good; the necessities of souls called to him, <hi type="italic">Come over, and help us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.9">Acts xvi. 9</reference>); he removed <hi type="italic">when he saw great multitudes about him.</hi> Though by this it appeared that they were desirous to have him there, he knew there were others as desirous to have him with them, and they must have their share of him: his being acceptable and useful in one place was no objection against, but a reason for, his going to another. Thus he would try the multitudes that were <hi type="italic">about him,</hi> whether their zeal would carry them to follow him, and attend on him, when his preaching was removed to some distance. Many would be glad of such helps, if they could have them at next door, who will not be at the pains to follow them to <hi type="italic">the other side;</hi> and thus Christ shook off those who were less zealous, and the perfect were made manifest. <div eID="gen21823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21824" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's communication with two, who, upon his remove to <hi type="italic">the other side,</hi> were loth to stay behind, and had a mind to follow him, not as others, who were his followers at large, but to come into close discipleship, which the most were shy of; for it carried such a face of strictness as they could not like, nor be well reconciled to; but here is an account of two who seemed desirous to come into communion, and yet were not right; which is here given as a specimen of the hindrances by which many are kept from closing with Christ, and cleaving to him; and a warning to us, to set out in following Christ, so as that we may not come short; to lay such a foundation, as that our building may stand. <div eID="gen21824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21825" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's managing of two different tempers, one quick and eager, the other dull and heavy; and his instructions are adapted to each of them, and designed for our use. <div eID="gen21825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21826" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is one that was <hi type="italic">too hasty in promising;</hi> and he was <hi type="italic">a certain scribe</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.19">v. 19</reference>), a scholar, a learned man, one of those that studied and expounded the law; generally we find them in the gospels to be men of no good character; usually coupled with the Pharisees, as enemies to Christ and his doctrine. <hi type="italic">Where is the scribe?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1 Cor. i. 20</reference>. He is very seldom following Christ; yet here was one that bid pretty fair for discipleship, a <hi type="italic">Saul among the prophets.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen21826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21827" type="x-p"/> (1.) How he expressed his forwardness; <hi type="italic">Master, I will follow thee, whithersoever thou goest.</hi> I know not how any man could have spoken better. His profession of a self-dedication to Christ is, [1.] Very ready, and seems to be <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—from his unbiased inclination:</hi> he is not called to it by Christ, nor urged by any of the disciples, but, of his own accord, he proffers himself to be a close follower of Christ; he is not a pressed man, but a volunteer. [2.] Very resolute; he seems to be at a point in this matter; he does not say, "I have a mind to <hi type="italic">follow thee;</hi>" but, "I am determined, <hi type="italic">I will</hi> do it." [3.] It was unlimited and without reserve; "<hi type="italic">I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest;</hi> not only to <hi type="italic">the other side</hi> of the country, but if it were to the utmost regions of the world." Now we should think ourselves sure of such a man as this; and yet it appears, by Christ's answer, that his resolution was rash, his ends low and carnal: either he did not consider at all, or not that which was to be considered; he saw the miracles Christ wrought, and hoped he would set up a temporal kingdom, and he wished to apply betimes for a share in it. Note, There are many resolutions for religion, produced by some sudden pangs of conviction, and taken up without due consideration, that prove abortive, and come to nothing: soon ripe, soon rotten. <div eID="gen21827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21828" type="x-p"/> (2.) How Christ tried his forwardness, whether it were sincere or not, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">v. 20</reference>. He let him know that this <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> whom he is so eager to follow, <hi type="italic">has not where to lay his head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">v. 20</reference>. Now from this account of Christ's deep poverty, we observe, <div eID="gen21828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21829" type="x-p"/> [1.] That it is strange in itself, that the Son of God, when he came into the world, should put himself into such a very low condition, as to want the convenience of a certain resting-place, which the meanest of the creatures have. If he would <hi type="italic">take our nature upon him,</hi> one would think, he should have taken it in its best estate and circumstances: no, he takes it in its worst. See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How well provided for the inferior creatures are: <hi type="italic">The foxes have holes;</hi> though they are not only not useful, but hurtful, to man, yet God provides holes for them in which they are earthed: man endeavours to destroy them, but thus they are sheltered; their holes are their castles. <hi type="italic">The birds of the air,</hi> though they take no care for themselves, yet are taken care of, and <hi type="italic">have nests</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.17">Ps. civ. 17</reference>); <hi type="italic">nests</hi> in the field; some of them <hi type="italic">nests</hi> in the house; in God's courts, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Ps. lxxxiv. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How poorly the Lord Jesus was provided for. It may encourage us to trust God for necessaries, that the beasts and birds have such good provision; and may comfort us, if we want necessaries, that our Master did so before us. Note, Our Lord Jesus, when he was here in the world, submitted to the disgraces and distresses of extreme poverty; <hi type="italic">for our sakes he became poor,</hi> very poor. He had not a settlement, had not a place of repose, not a house of his own, to put his head in, not a pillow of his own, to lay his head on. He and his disciples lived upon the charity of well-disposed people, that <hi type="italic">ministered to him of their substance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.8.2">Luke viii. 2</reference>. Christ submitted to this, not only that he might in all respects humble himself, and fulfil the scriptures, which spake of him as <hi type="italic">poor and needy,</hi> but that he might show us the vanity of worldly wealth, and teach us to look upon it with a holy contempt; that he might purchase better things for us, and so <hi type="italic">make us rich,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2 Cor. viii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen21829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21830" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is strange that such a declaration should be made on this occasion. When a scribe offered to follow Christ, one would think he would have encouraged him, and said, <hi type="italic">Come, and I will take care of thee;</hi> one scribe might be capable of doing him more credit and service than twelve fishermen: but Christ saw his heart, and answered to the thoughts of that, and therein teaches us all how to come to Christ. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The scribe's resolve seems to have been sudden; and Christ would have us, when we take upon us a profession of religion, to <hi type="italic">sit down and count the cost</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.28">Luke xiv. 28</reference>), to do it intelligently, and with consideration, and choose the way of godliness, not because we know no other, but because we know no better. It is no advantage to religion, to take men by surprise, ere they are aware. They that take up a profession <hi type="italic">in a pang,</hi> will throw it off again <hi type="italic">in a fret;</hi> let them, therefore, <hi type="italic">take time,</hi> and they will have <hi type="italic">done the sooner:</hi> let him that will follow Christ know the worst of it, and expect to lie hard, and fare hard. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His resolve seems to have been from a worldly, covetous principle. He saw what abundance of cures Christ wrought, and concluded that he had large fees, and would get an estate quickly, and therefore he would follow him in hopes of growing rich with him; but Christ rectifies his mistake, and tells him, he was so far from growing rich, that he had not a place to <hi type="italic">lay his head on;</hi> and that if he follow him, he cannot expect to fare better than he fared. Note, Christ will accept none for his followers that aim at worldly advantages in following him, or design to make any thing but heaven of their religion. We have reason to think that this scribe, hereupon, <hi type="italic">went away sorrowful,</hi> being disappointed in a bargain which he thought would turn to account; he is not for following Christ, unless he can <hi type="italic">get by him.</hi> <div eID="gen21830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21831" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is another that was too <hi type="italic">slow in performing.</hi> Delay in execution is as bad, on the one hand, as precipitancy in resolution is on the other hand; when we have taken time to consider, and then have determined, let it never be said, we left that to be done to-morrow, which we could do to-day. This candidate for the ministry was one of Christ's disciples already (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.21">v. 21</reference>), a follower of him at large. Clemens Alexandrinus tells us, from an ancient tradition, that this was Philip; he seems to be better qualified and disposed than the former; because not so confident and presumptuous: a bold, eager, over-forward temper is not the most promising in religion; sometimes the last are first, and the first last. Now observe here, <div eID="gen21831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21832" type="x-p"/> (1.) The excuse that this disciple made, to defer an immediate attendance on Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.21">v. 21</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.</hi> Before I come to be a close and constant follower of thee, let me be allowed to perform this last office of respect to my father; and in the mean time, let it suffice to be a hearer of thee now and then, when I can spare time." His father (some think) was now sick, or dying, or dead; others think, he was only aged, and not likely in a course of nature, to continue long; and he desired leave to attend upon him in his sickness, at his death, and to his grave, and then he would be at Christ's service. This seemed a reasonable request, and yet it was not right. He had not the zeal he should have had for the work, and therefore pleaded this, because it seemed a plausible plea. Note, An unwilling mind never wants an excuse. The meaning of <hi type="italic">Non vacat</hi> is, <hi type="italic">Non placet—The want of leisure is the want of inclination.</hi> We will suppose it to come from a true filial affection and respect for his father, yet still the preference should have been given to Christ. Note, Many are hindered <hi type="italic">from</hi> and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the way of serious godliness, by an over-concern for their families and relations; these lawful things undo us all, and our duty to God is neglected, and postponed, under colour of discharging our debts to the world; here therefore we have need to double our guard. <div eID="gen21832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21833" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ's disallowing of this excuse (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">Jesus said to him, Follow me;</hi> and, no doubt, power accompanied this word to him, as to others, and he did <hi type="italic">follow Christ,</hi> and cleaved to him, as Ruth to Naomi, when the scribe, in the <reference osisRef="Matt.8.19-Matt.8.20">verses before</reference>, like Orpah, took leave of him. That said, <hi type="italic">I will follow thee;</hi> to this Christ said, <hi type="italic">Follow me;</hi> comparing them together, it is intimated that we are brought to Christ by the force of his call to us, not of our promises to him; it is <hi type="italic">not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy;</hi> he calls whom he will, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.16">Rom. ix. 16</reference>. And further, Note, Though chosen vessels may make excuses, and delay their compliance with divine calls a great while, yet Christ will at length answer their excuses, conquer their unwillingness, and bring them to his feet; when Christ calls, he will overcome, and make the call effectual, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.10">1 Sam. iii. 10</reference>. His excuse is laid aside as insufficient; <hi type="italic">Let the dead bury their dead.</hi> It is a proverbial expression; "Let one dead man bury another: rather let them lie unburied, than that the service of Christ should be neglected. <hi type="italic">Let the dead</hi> spiritually <hi type="italic">bury the dead</hi> corporally; let worldly offices be left to worldly people; do not thou encumber thyself with them. Burying the dead, and especially a dead father, is a good work, but it is not thy work at this time: it may be done as well by others, that are not called and qualified, as thou art, to be employed for Christ; thou hast something else to do, and must not defer that." Note, Piety to God must be preferred before piety to parents, though that is a great and needful part of our religion. The Nazarites, under the law, were not to mourn for their own parents, because they were <hi type="italic">holy to the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.6.6-Num.6.8">Num. vi. 6-8</reference>); nor was the high priest to <hi type="italic">defile himself for the dead,</hi> no, not for <hi type="italic">his own father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.21.11-Lev.21.12">Lev. xxi. 11, 12</reference>. And Christ requires of those who would follow him, that they <hi type="italic">hate father and mother</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>); love them less than God; we must comparatively neglect and disesteem our nearest relations, when they come in competition with Christ, and either our doing for him, or our suffering for him.
entries.c0e0d5d0171443a97134c211bd68c90fe261a2cb: <div eID="gen21833" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jesus Allays a Storm.</title> <div sID="gen21834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And when he was entered into a ship, his disciples followed him. <hi type="super">24</hi> And, behold, there arose a great tempest in the sea, insomuch that the ship was covered with the waves: but he was asleep. <hi type="super">25</hi> And his disciples came to <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and awoke him, saying, Lord, save us: we perish. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm. <hi type="super">27</hi> But the men marvelled, saying, What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him! <div eID="gen21834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21835" type="x-p"/> Christ had given sailing orders to his disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.18">v. 18</reference>), that they should <hi type="italic">depart to the other side of the sea of Tiberias,</hi> into the country of Gadara, in the tribe of Gad, which lay east of Jordan; thither he would go to rescue a poor creature that was possessed <hi type="italic">with a legion of devils,</hi> though he foresaw how he should be affronted there. Now. 1. He chose to go by water. It had not been much about, if he had gone by land; but he chose to cross the lake, that he might have occasion to manifest himself the God <hi type="italic">of the sea</hi> as well as of <hi type="italic">the dry land,</hi> and to show that <hi type="italic">all power is his, both in heaven and in earth.</hi> It is a comfort to those <hi type="italic">who go down to the sea in ships,</hi> and are often in perils there, to reflect that they have a Saviour to trust in, and pray to, who knows what it is to be at sea, and to be in storms there. But observe, when he went to sea, he had no yacht or pleasure-boat to attend him, but made use of his disciples' fishing-boats; so poorly was he accommodated in all respects. 2. <hi type="italic">His disciples followed him;</hi> the twelve kept close to him, when others staid behind upon the <hi type="italic">terra firma,</hi> where there was sure footing. Note, They, and they only, will be found the true disciples of Christ, that are willing to go to sea with him, to follow him into dangers and difficulties. Many would be content to go the land-way to heaven, that will rather stand still, or go back, than venture upon a dangerous sea; but those that would rest with Christ hereafter must follow him now wherever he leads them, into a ship or into a prison, as well as into a palace. Now observe here, <div eID="gen21835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21836" type="x-p"/> I. The peril and perplexity of the disciples in this voyage; and in this appeared the truth of what Christ had just now said, that those who follow him must count upon difficulties, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen21836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21837" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">There arose a very great storm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.24">v. 24</reference>. Christ could have prevented this storm, and have ordered them a pleasant passage, but that would not have been so much for his glory and the confirmation of their faith as their deliverance was: this storm was <hi type="italic">for their sakes,</hi> as <reference osisRef="John.11.4">John xi. 4</reference>. One would have expected, that having Christ with them, they should have had a very favourable gale, but it is quite otherwise; for Christ would show that they who are passing with him over the ocean of this world to the other side, must expect storms by the way. The church is <hi type="italic">tossed with tempests</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.11">Isa. liv. 11</reference>); it is only the upper region that enjoys a perpetual calm, this lower one is ever and anon disturbed and disturbing. <div eID="gen21837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21838" type="x-p"/> 2. Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">was asleep in this storm.</hi> We never read of Christ's sleeping but at this time; he was in watchings often, and continued all night in prayer to God: this was a sleep, not of security, like Jonah's in a storm, but of holy serenity, and dependence upon his Father: he slept to show that he was really and truly man, and subject to the sinless infirmities of our nature: his work made him weary and sleepy, and he had no guilt, no fear within, to disturb his repose. Those that can lay their heads upon the pillow of a clear conscience, may sleep quietly and sweetly in a storm (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Ps. iv. 8</reference>), as Peter, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.6">Acts xii. 6</reference>. He slept at this time, to try the faith of his disciples, whether they could trust him when he seemed to slight them. He slept not so much with a desire to be refreshed, as with a design to be awaked. <div eID="gen21838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21839" type="x-p"/> 3. The poor disciples, though used to the sea, were in a great fright, and in their fear <hi type="italic">came to</hi> their Master, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.25">v. 25</reference>. Whither else should they go? It was well they had him so near them. They <hi type="italic">awoke him</hi> with their prayers; <hi type="italic">Lord, save us, we perish.</hi> Note, They who would learn to pray must go to sea. Imminent and sensible dangers will drive people to him who alone can help in time of need. Their prayer has life in it, <hi type="italic">Lord, save us, we perish.</hi> (1.) Their petition is, <hi type="italic">Lord, save us.</hi> They believed he <hi type="italic">could</hi> save them; they begged he <hi type="italic">would,</hi> Christ's errand into the world was <hi type="italic">to save,</hi> but those only <hi type="italic">shall be saved that call on the name of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.21">Acts ii. 21</reference>. They who by faith are interested in the eternal salvation wrought out by Christ, may with a humble confidence apply themselves to him for temporal deliverances. Observe, They call him, <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> and then pray, <hi type="italic">Save us.</hi> Note, Christ will save none but those that are willing to take him for their Lord; for he is a Prince and a Saviour. (2.) Their plea is, <hi type="italic">We perish;</hi> which was, [1.] The language of their fear; they looked upon their case as desperate, and gave up all for lost; they had received a sentence of death within themselves, and this they plead, "<hi type="italic">We perish,</hi> if thou dost not save us; look upon us therefore with pity." [2.] It was the language of their fervency; they pray as men in earnest, that beg for their lives; it becomes us thus to strive and wrestle in prayer; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> Christ slept, that he might draw out this importunity. <div eID="gen21839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21840" type="x-p"/> II. The power and grace of Jesus Christ put forth for their succour: then the Lord Jesus awaked, as one refreshed, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Ps. lxxviii. 65</reference>.
