Christ may sleep when his church is in a storm, but he will not outsleep himself: the time, the set time to favour his distressed church, will come, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Ps. cii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen21840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21841" type="x-p"/> 1. He rebuked the disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.26">v. 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?</hi> He does not chide them for disturbing him with their prayers, but for disturbing themselves with their fears. Christ reproved them first, and then delivered them; this is his method, to prepare us for a mercy, and then to give it us. Observe, (1.) His dislike of their fears; "<hi type="italic">Why are ye fearful?</hi> Ye, my disciples? Let the sinners in Zion be afraid, let heathen mariners tremble in a storm, but you shall not be so. Enquire into the reasons of your fear, and weigh them." (2.) His discovery of the cause and spring of their fears; <hi type="italic">O ye of little faith.</hi> Many that have true faith are weak in it, and it does but little. Note, [1.] Christ's disciples are apt to be disquieted with fears in a stormy day, to torment themselves with jealousies that things are bad with them, and dismal conclusions that they will be worse. [2.] The prevalence of our inordinate fears in a stormy day is owing to the weakness of our faith, which would be as an anchor to the soul, and would ply the oar of prayer. By faith we might see through the storm to the quiet shore, and encourage ourselves with hope that we shall weather our point. [3.] The fearfulness of Christ's disciples in a storm, and their unbelief, the cause of it, are very displeasing to the Lord Jesus, for they reflect dishonour upon him, and create disturbance to themselves. <div eID="gen21841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21842" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">rebukes the wind;</hi> the former he did as the God of <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> and the Sovereign of the heart, who can do what he pleases <hi type="italic">in</hi> us; this he did as the God of <hi type="italic">nature,</hi> the Sovereign of the world, who can do what he pleases <hi type="italic">for</hi> us. It is the same <hi type="italic">power that stills the noise of the sea,</hi> and the tumult of fear, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">Ps. lxv. 7</reference>. See, (1.) How <hi type="italic">easily</hi> this was done, with a word's speaking. Moses commanded the waters with a rod; Joshua, with the ark of the covenant; Elisha, with the prophet's mantle; but Christ with a word. See his absolute dominion over all the creatures, which bespeaks both his honour, and the happiness of those that have him on their side. (2.) How <hi type="italic">effectually</hi> it was done? <hi type="italic">There was a great calm,</hi> all of a sudden. Ordinarily, after a storm, there is such a fret of the waters, that it is a good while ere they can settle; but if Christ speak the word, not only the storm ceases, but all the effects of it, all the remains of it. Great storms of doubt, and fear in the soul, under the power of the spirit of bondage, sometimes end in a wonderful calm, created and spoken by the Spirit of adoption. <div eID="gen21842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21843" type="x-p"/> 3. This excited their astonishment (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.27">v. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">The men marvelled.</hi> They had been long acquainted with the sea, and never saw a storm so immediately turned into a perfect calm, in all their lives. It has all the marks and signatures of a miracle upon it; <hi type="italic">it is the Lord's doing, and is marvellous in their eyes.</hi> Observe, (1.) Their admiration of Christ; <hi type="italic">What manner of man is this!</hi> Note, Christ is a Nonsuch; every thing in him is admirable: none so wise, so mighty, so amiable, as he. (2.) The reason of it; <hi type="italic">Even the winds and the sea obey him.</hi> Upon this account, Christ is to be admired, that he has a commanding power even over <hi type="italic">winds and seas.</hi> Others pretended to cure diseases, but he only undertook to command <hi type="italic">the winds.</hi> We know not the way of <hi type="italic">the wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.8">John iii. 8</reference>), much less can we control it; but he that <hi type="italic">bringeth forth the wind out of his treasury</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>), when it is out, gathers it into his fists, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Prov. xxx. 4</reference>. He that can do this, can do any thing, can do enough to encourage our confidence and comfort in him, in the most stormy day, within or without, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Isa. xxvi. 4</reference>. The Lord <hi type="italic">sits upon the floods,</hi> and is <hi type="italic">mightier than the noise of many waters.</hi> Christ, by commanding <hi type="italic">the seas,</hi> showed himself to be the same that <hi type="italic">made the world, when, at his rebuke, the waters fled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.7-Ps.104.8">Ps. civ. 7, 8</reference>), as now, <hi type="italic">at his rebuke,</hi> they fell.
entries.f6fb044c04cf21e6e9129831e3519173098e0877: <div eID="gen21843" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Devils Cast Out of Two Men.</title> <div sID="gen21844" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way. <hi type="super">29</hi> And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time? <hi type="super">30</hi> And there was a good way off from them a herd of many swine feeding. <hi type="super">31</hi> So the devils besought him, saying, If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he said unto them, Go. And when they were come out, they went into the herd of swine: and, behold, the whole herd of swine ran violently down a steep place into the sea, and perished in the waters. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they that kept them fled, and went their ways into the city, and told every thing, and what was befallen to the possessed of the devils. <hi type="super">34</hi> And, behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus: and when they saw him, they besought <hi type="italic">him</hi> that he would depart out of their coasts. <div eID="gen21844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21845" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of Christ's casting the devils out of two men that were possessed. The scope of this chapter is to show the divine power of Christ, by the instances of his dominion over bodily diseases, which to us are irresistible; over winds and waves, which to us are yet more uncontrollable; and lastly, over devils, which to us are most formidable of all. Christ has not only all <hi type="italic">power in heaven and earth</hi> and all deep places, but has the keys of hell too. <hi type="italic">Principalities and powers were made subject to him,</hi> even while he was in his estate of humiliation, as an earnest of what should be at his entrance into his glory (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Eph. i. 21</reference>); he spoiled them, <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. It was observed in general (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.16">v. 16</reference>), that Christ <hi type="italic">cast out the spirits with his word;</hi> here we have a particular instance of it, which have some circumstances more remarkable than the rest. This miracle was wrought in the country of the Gergesenes; some think, they were the remains of the old Girgashites, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deut. vii. 1</reference>. Though Christ was sent chiefly <hi type="italic">to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,</hi> yet some sallies he made among the borderers, as here, to gain this victory over Satan, which was a specimen of the conquest of his legions in the Gentile world. <div eID="gen21845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21846" type="x-p"/> Now, besides the general instance which this gives us of Christ's power over Satan, and his design against him to disarm and dispossess him, we have here especially discovered to us the way and manner of evil spirits in their enmity to man. Observe, concerning this legion of devils, What work they made where they <hi type="italic">were,</hi> and where they <hi type="italic">went.</hi> <div eID="gen21846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21847" type="x-p"/> I. What work they made where they <hi type="italic">were;</hi> which appears in the miserable condition of these two that were possessed by them; and some think, these two were man and wife, because the other Evangelists speak but of one. <div eID="gen21847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21848" type="x-p"/> 1. They dwelt among <hi type="italic">the tombs;</hi> thence they came when the met Christ. The devil having <hi type="italic">the power of death,</hi> not as judge, but as executioner, he delighted to converse among the trophies of his victory, the dead bodies of men; but there, where he thought himself in the greatest triumph and elevation, as afterwards in Golgotha, the place of a skull, did Christ conquer and subdue him. Conversing among the graves increased the melancholy and frenzy of the poor possessed creatures, and so strengthened the hold he had of them by their bodily distemper, and also made them more formidable to other people, who generally startle at any thing that stirs among <hi type="italic">the tombs.</hi> <div eID="gen21848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21849" type="x-p"/> 2. They were <hi type="italic">exceeding fierce;</hi> not only ungovernable themselves, but mischievous to others, frightening many, having hurt some; <hi type="italic">so that no man durst pass that way.</hi> Note, The devil bears malice to mankind, and shows it by making men spiteful and malicious one to another. Mutual enmities, where they should be mutual endearments and assistances, are effects and evidences of Satan's enmity to the whole race; he makes one man a wolf, a bear, a devil, to another—<hi type="italic">Homo homini lupus.</hi> Where Satan rules in a man spiritually, by those lusts that war in the members, pride, envy, malice, revenge, they make him as unfit for human society, as unworthy of it, and as much an enemy to the comfort of it, as these poor possessed creatures were. <div eID="gen21849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21850" type="x-p"/> 3. They bid defiance to Jesus Christ, and disclaimed all interest in him, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">v. 29</reference>. It is an instance of the power of God over the devils, that, notwithstanding the mischief they studied to do <hi type="italic">by</hi> and <hi type="italic">to</hi> these poor creatures, yet they could not keep them from meeting Jesus Christ, who ordered the matter so as to meet them. It was his overpowering hand that dragged these unclean spirits into his presence, which they dreaded more than any thing else: his chains could hold them, when the chains that men made for them could not. But being brought before him, they protested against his jurisdiction, and broke out into a rage, <hi type="italic">What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God?</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen21850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21851" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">One</hi> word that the devil spoke like a <hi type="italic">saint;</hi> he addressed himself to Christ as <hi type="italic">Jesus the Son of God;</hi> a <hi type="italic">good</hi> word, and at this time, when it was a truth but in the proving, it was a <hi type="italic">great</hi> word too, what flesh and blood did not reveal to Peter, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">ch. xvi. 17</reference>. Even the devils know, and believe, and confess Christ to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and yet they are devils still, which makes their enmity to Christ so much the more wicked, and indeed a perfect torment to themselves; for how can it be otherwise, to oppose one they know to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God?</hi> Note, It is not knowledge, but love, that distinguishes saints from devils. He is the first-born of hell, that knows Christ and yet hates him, and will not be subject to him and his law. We may remember that not long since the devil made a doubt whether Christ were <hi type="italic">the Son of God</hi> or not, and would have persuaded him to question it (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.3">ch. iv. 3</reference>), but now he readily owns it. Note, Though God's children may be much disquieted in an hour of temptation, by Satan's questioning their relation to God as a Father, yet the Spirit of adoption shall at length clear it up to them so much to their satisfaction, as to set it even above the devil's contradiction. <div eID="gen21851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21852" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Two</hi> words that he said like a <hi type="italic">devil,</hi> like himself. <div eID="gen21852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21853" type="x-p"/> [1.] A word of defiance; <hi type="italic">What have we to do with thee?</hi> Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is true that the devils have nothing to do with Christ as a Saviour, <hi type="italic">for he took not on him the nature of the angels</hi> that fell, nor did he lay hold on them (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.16">Heb. ii. 16</reference>); they are in no relation to him, they neither have, nor hope for, any benefit by him. O the depth of this mystery of divine love, that fallen man hath so much <hi type="italic">to do with Christ,</hi> when fallen angels have nothing <hi type="italic">to do with</hi> him! Surely here was torment enough before the time, to be forced to own the excellency <hi type="italic">that is in Christ,</hi> and yet that he has no interest in him. Note, It is possible for me to call Jesus <hi type="italic">the Son of God,</hi> and yet have nothing to do with him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is as true, that the devils desire not to have any thing <hi type="italic">to do with Christ</hi> as a Ruler; they hate him, they are filled with enmity against him, they stand in opposition to him, and are in open rebellion against his crown and dignity. See whose language they speak, that will have nothing <hi type="italic">to do with the</hi> gospel of Christ, with his laws and ordinances, that throw off his yoke, that <hi type="italic">break his bands in sunder,</hi> and <hi type="italic">will not have him to reign over them;</hi> that say <hi type="italic">to the Almighty</hi> Jesus, <hi type="italic">Depart from us: they are of their father the devil, they do his lusts,</hi> and speak his language. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> But it is not true, that the devils have nothing <hi type="italic">to do with Christ</hi> as a Judge, for they have, and they know it. These devils could not say, <hi type="italic">What hast thou to do with us?</hi> could not deny that the Son of God is the Judge of devils; to his judgment they are bound over in chains of darkness, which they would fain shake off, and shake off the thought of. <div eID="gen21853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21854" type="x-p"/> [2.] A word of dread and deprecation; "<hi type="italic">Art thou come hither to torment us</hi>—to cast us out from these men, and to restrain us from doing the hurt we would do?" Note, To be turned out, and tied up, from doing mischief, is a torment to the devil, all whose comfort and satisfaction are man's misery and destruction. Should not we then count it our heaven to be doing well, and reckon that our torment, whether within or without, that hinders us from well-doing? Now must we be tormented by thee <hi type="italic">before the time;</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There is a time in which devils will be more tormented than they are, and they know it. The great assize at the last day is the time fixed for their complete torture, in that Tophet which is ordained of old <hi type="italic">for the king, for the prince of the devils, and his angels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">Matt. xxv. 41</reference>); <hi type="italic">for the judgment of that day</hi> they are <hi type="italic">reserved,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2 Pet. ii. 4</reference>. Those malignant spirits that are, by the divine permission, prisoners <hi type="italic">at large,</hi> walking to and fro through the earth (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), are even now in a chain; hitherto shall their power reach, and no further; they will then be made <hi type="italic">close</hi> prisoners: they have now some ease; they will then be in torment without ease. This they here take for granted, and ask not never to be tormented (despair of relief is the misery of their case), but they beg that they may not be tormented <hi type="italic">before the time;</hi> for though they knew not when the day of judgment should be, they knew it should not be yet. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The devils have <hi type="italic">a certain fearful looking for of that judgment and fiery indignation,</hi> upon every approach of Christ, and every check that is given to their power and rage. The very sight of Christ and his word of command to come out of the man, made them thus apprehensive of their torment. Thus <hi type="italic">the devils believe, and tremble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.19">Jam. ii. 19</reference>. It is their own enmity to God and man that puts them upon the rack, and <hi type="italic">torments them before the time.</hi> The most desperate sinners, whose damnation is sealed, yet cannot quite harden their hearts against the surprise of fearfulness, <hi type="italic">when they see the day approaching.</hi> <div eID="gen21854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21855" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now see what work they made where they <hi type="italic">went,</hi> when they were turned out of the men possessed, and that was into <hi type="italic">a herd of swine,</hi> which <hi type="italic">was a good way off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.30">v. 30</reference>. These Gergesenes, though living on the other side Jordan, were Jews. What had they to do with <hi type="italic">swine,</hi> which by the law were unclean, and not to be eaten nor touched? Probably, lying in the outskirts of the land, there were many Gentiles among them, to whom this <hi type="italic">herd of swine</hi> belonged: or they kept them to be sold, or bartered, to the Romans, with whom they had now great dealings, and who were admirers of <hi type="italic">swine's</hi> flesh. Now observe, <div eID="gen21855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21856" type="x-p"/> 1. How the devils seized the <hi type="italic">swine.</hi> Though they were <hi type="italic">a good way off,</hi> and, one would think, out of danger, yet the devils had an eye upon them, to do them a mischief: for they <hi type="italic">go up and down, seeking to devour,</hi> seeking an opportunity; and they seek not long but they find. Now here, <div eID="gen21856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21857" type="x-p"/> (1.) They <hi type="italic">asked</hi> leave to enter <hi type="italic">into the swine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.31">v. 31</reference>); <hi type="italic">they besought him,</hi> with all earnestness, <hi type="italic">If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine.</hi> Hereby, [1.] They discover their own inclination to do mischief, and what a pleasure it is to them; those, therefore, are their children, and resemble them, <hi type="italic">whose sleep departeth from them, except they cause some to fall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Prov. iv. 16</reference>. "Let us go <hi type="italic">into the herd of swine,</hi> any where rather than into the place of torment, any where to do mischief." If they might not be suffered to hurt men in their bodies, they would hurt them in their goods, and in that too they intend hurt to their souls, by making Christ a burthen to them: such malicious devices hath that old subtle serpent! [2.] They own Christ's power over them; that, without his sufferance and permission, they could not so much as hurt a <hi type="italic">swine.</hi> This is comfortable to all the Lord's people, that, though the devil's power be very great, yet it is limited, and not equal to his malice (what would become of us, if it were?) especially that it is under the control of our Lord Jesus, our most faithful, powerful friend and Saviour; that Satan and his instruments can go no further than he is pleased to permit; <hi type="italic">here shall their proud waves be stayed.</hi> <div eID="gen21857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21858" type="x-p"/> (2.) They <hi type="italic">had</hi> leave. Christ said unto them, <hi type="italic">Go</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.32">v. 32</reference>), as God did to Satan, when he desired leave to afflict Job. Note, God does often, for wise and holy ends, permit the efforts of Satan's rage, and suffer him to do the mischief he would, and even by it serve his own purposes. The devils are not only Christ's captives, but his vassals; his dominion over them appears in the harm they do, as well as in the hindrance of them from doing more. Thus even their wrath is made to praise Christ, and the remainder of it he does and will restrain. Christ permitted this, [1.] For the conviction of the Sadducees that were then among the Jews, who denied the existence of spirits, and would not own that there were such beings, because they could not see them. Now Christ would, by this, bring it as near as might be to an ocular demonstration of the being, multitude, power, and malice, of evil spirits, that, if they were not hereby convinced, they might be left inexcusable in their infidelity. We see not the wind, but it would be absurd to deny it, when we see trees and houses blown down by it. [2.] For the punishment of the Gadarenes, who perhaps, though Jews, took a liberty to eat <hi type="italic">swine's</hi> flesh, contrary to the law: however, their keeping <hi type="italic">swine</hi> bordered upon evil; and Christ would also show what a hellish crew they were delivered from, which, if he had permitted it, would soon have choked them, as they did their <hi type="italic">swine.</hi> The devils, in obedience to Christ's command, came out of the men, and having permission, <hi type="italic">when they were come out, immediately they went into the herd of swine.</hi> See what an industrious enemy Satan is, and how expeditious; he will lose no time in doing mischief. Observe, <div eID="gen21858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21859" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Whither they hurried them,</hi> when they had seized them. They were not bid to <hi type="italic">save their lives,</hi> and, therefore, they were made to <hi type="italic">run violently down a steep place into the sea,</hi> where they all perished, to the number of about <hi type="italic">two thousand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.13">Mark v. 13</reference>. Note, The possession which the devil gets is for destruction. Thus the devil hurries people to sin, hurries them to that which they have resolved against, and which they know will be shame and grief to them: with what a force doth the evil spirit <hi type="italic">work in the children of disobedience,</hi> when by so many foolish and hurtful lusts they are brought to act in direct contradiction, not only to religion, but to right reason, and their interest in this world! Thus, likewise, he hurries them to ruin, for he is Apollyon and Abaddon, the great destroyer. By his lusts which men do, they are <hi type="italic">drowned in destruction and perdition.</hi> This is Satan's will, to <hi type="italic">swallow up</hi> and to <hi type="italic">devour;</hi> miserable then is the condition of those that are led <hi type="italic">captive by him at his will.</hi> They are hurried into a worse lake than this, a lake that <hi type="italic">burns with fire and brimstone.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen21859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21860" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">What effect this had upon the owners.</hi> The report of it was soon brought them by the swine-herds, who seemed to be more concerned for the loss of the swine than any thing else, for they went not to tell <hi type="italic">what was befallen to the possessed of the devils,</hi> till the swine were lost, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.33">v. 33</reference>. Christ went not <hi type="italic">into the city,</hi> but the news of his being there did, by which he was willing to feel how their pulse beat, and what influence it had upon them, and then act accordingly. <div eID="gen21860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21861" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) Their curiosity brought them out to see Jesus. The <hi type="italic">whole city came out to meet him,</hi> that they might be able to say, they had seen a man who did such wonderful works. Thus many go out, in profession, to meet Christ for company, that have no real affection for him, nor desire to know him. <div eID="gen21861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21862" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their covetousness made them <hi type="italic">willing to be rid of him.</hi> Instead of inviting him into their city, or bringing their sick to him to be healed, they desired him <hi type="italic">to depart out of their coasts,</hi> as if they had borrowed the words of the devils, <hi type="italic">What have we to do with thee, Jesus thou Son of God?</hi> And now the devils had what they aimed at in drowning the swine; <hi type="italic">they</hi> did it, and then made the people believe that <hi type="italic">Christ</hi> had done it, and so prejudiced them against him. He seduced our first parents, by possessing them with hard thoughts of God, and kept the Gadarenes from Christ, by suggesting that he came into their country to destroy their cattle, and that he would do more hurt than good; for though he had cured two men, yet he had drowned two thousand swine. Thus the devil sows tares in God's field, does mischief in the Christian church, and then lays the blame upon Christianity, and incenses men against that. They besought him that he would depart, lest, like Moses in Egypt, he should proceed to some other plague. Note, There are a great many who prefer their swine before their Saviour, and so come short of Christ, and salvation by him. They desire Christ to depart out of their hearts, and will not suffer his word to have a place in them, because he and his word will be the destruction of their brutish lusts—those swine which they give up themselves to feed. And justly will Christ forsake those that thus are weary of him, and say to them hereafter, <hi type="italic">Depart, ye cursed,</hi> who now say to the Almighty, <hi type="italic">Depart from us.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.8"/> <div eID="gen21862" type="x-p"/>

entries.37efa52ebe6a7715d8aac7e66bd7e68a610457c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13462"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">Mt 8:1-4</reference>. Healing of a Leper. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.1.40-Mark.1.45">Mr 1:40-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.12-Luke.5.16">Lu 5:12-16</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> The time of this miracle seems too definitely fixed here to admit of our placing it where it stands in Mark and Luke, in whose Gospels no such precise note of time is given.<div eID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13462"/>1. When he was come down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him. <div eID="gen25700" type="x-p"/>
entries.d25a18fe3d99fb9a9ac7d5f6058a2502f6d1575b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13463"/><div sID="gen25701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13463"/><hi type="bold">2. And, behold, there came a leper--</hi>"a man full of leprosy," says <reference osisRef="Luke.5.12">Lu 5:12</reference>. Much has been written on this disease of leprosy, but certain points remain still doubtful. All that needs be said here is that it was a cutaneous disease, of a loathsome, diffusive, and, there is reason to believe, when thoroughly pronounced, incurable character; that though in its distinctive features it is still found in several countries--as Arabia, Egypt, and South Africa--it prevailed, in the form of what is called white leprosy, to an unusual extent, and from a very early period, among the Hebrews; and that it thus furnished to the whole nation a familiar and affecting symbol of SIN, considered as (1) loathsome, (2) spreading, (3) incurable. And while the ceremonial ordinances for detection and cleansing prescribed in this case by the law of Moses (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.14.57">Le 13:1-14:57</reference>) held forth a coming remedy "for sin and for uncleanness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.7">Psa 51:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.1">2Ki 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.10">7, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.14">13, 14</reference>), the numerous cases of leprosy with which our Lord came in contact, and the glorious cures of them which He wrought, were a fitting manifestation of the work which He came to accomplish. In this view, it deserves to be noticed that the first of our Lord's miracles of healing recorded by Matthew is this cure of a leper.<div eID="gen25701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and worshipped him--</hi>in what sense we shall presently see. Mark says (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.40">Mr 1:40</reference>), he came, "beseeching and kneeling to Him," and Luke says (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.12">Lu 5:12</reference>), "he fell on his face."<div eID="gen25702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean--</hi>As this is the only cure of leprosy recorded by all the three first Evangelists, it was probably the first case of the kind; and if so, this leper's faith in the power of Christ must have been formed in him by what he had heard of His other cures. And how striking a faith is it! He does not say he believed Him able, but with a brevity expressive of a confidence that knew no doubt, he says simply, "Thou canst." But of Christ's willingness to heal him he was not so sure. It needed more knowledge of Jesus than he could be supposed to have to assure him of that. But one thing he was sure of, that He had but to "will" it. This shows with what "worship" of Christ this leper fell on his face before Him. Clear theological knowledge of the Person of Christ was not then possessed even by those who were most with Him and nearest to Him. Much less could full insight into all that we know of the Only-begotten of the Father be expected of this leper. But he who at that moment felt and owned that to heal an incurable disease needed but the fiat of the Person who stood before him, had assuredly that very faith in the germ which now casts its crown before Him that loved us, and would at any time die for His blessed name. <div eID="gen25703" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d72357a42ad1131e8168774196c9ca76c50cc92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13464"/><div sID="gen25704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13464"/><hi type="bold">3. And Jesus--</hi>or "He," according to another reading,--"moved with compassion," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.41">Mr 1:41</reference>); a precious addition.<div eID="gen25704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put forth his hand, and touched him--</hi>Such a touch occasioned ceremonial defilement (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.3">Le 5:3</reference>); even as the leper's coming near enough for contact was against the Levitical regulations (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">Le 13:46</reference>). But as the man's faith told him there would be no case for such regulations if the cure he hoped to experience should be accomplished, so He who had healing in His wings transcended all such statutes.<div eID="gen25705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, I will; be thou clean--</hi>How majestic those two words! By not assuring the man of His power to heal him, He delightfully sets His seal to the man's previous confession of that power; and by assuring him of the one thing of which he had any doubt, and for which he waited--His will to do it--He makes a claim as divine as the cure which immediately followed it.<div eID="gen25706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And immediately his leprosy was cleansed--</hi>Mark, more emphatic, says (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.42">Mr 1:42</reference>), "And as soon as He had spoken, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was cleansed"--as perfectly as instantaneously. What a contrast this to modern pretended cures! <div eID="gen25707" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c3e243266982f6c7ae6ac5a1647b742ea3a2ba3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13465"/><div sID="gen25708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13465"/><hi type="bold">4. And Jesus--</hi>"straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.43">Mr 1:43</reference>), and<div eID="gen25708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saith unto him, See thou tell no man--</hi>A hard condition this would seem to a grateful heart, whose natural language, in such a case, is "Come, hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what He hath done for my soul" (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Psa 66:16</reference>). We shall presently see the reason for it.<div eID="gen25709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but go thy way, show thyself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.14.1-Lev.14.57">Le 14:1-57</reference>).<div eID="gen25710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a testimony unto them--</hi>a palpable witness that the Great Healer had indeed come, and that "God had visited His people." What the sequel was, our Evangelist Matthew does not say; but Mark thus gives it (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.45">Mr 1:45</reference>): "But he went out, and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter, insomuch that Jesus could no more openly enter into the city, but was without in desert places: and they came to Him from every quarter." Thus--by an over-zealous, though most natural and not very culpable, infringement of the injunction to keep the matter quiet--was our Lord, to some extent, thwarted in His movements. As His whole course was sublimely noiseless (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.19">Mt 12:19</reference>), so we find Him repeatedly taking steps to prevent matters prematurely coming to a crisis with Him. (But see on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.19">Mr 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">20</reference>). "And He withdrew Himself," adds Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.16">Lu 5:16</reference>), "into the wilderness, and prayed"; retreating from the popular excitement into the secret place of the Most High, and thus coming forth as dew upon the mown grass, and as showers that water the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference>). And this is the secret both of strength and of sweetness in the servants and followers of Christ in every age.<div eID="gen25711" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.5-Matt.8.13">Mt 8:5-13</reference>. Healing of the Centurion's Servant. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.7.1-Luke.7.10">Lu 7:1-10</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25712" type="x-p"/> This incident belongs to a later stage. For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.7.1-Luke.7.10">Lu 7:1-10</reference>.<div eID="gen25712" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.14-Matt.8.17">Mt 8:14-17</reference>. Healing of Peter's Mother-in-law and Many Others. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.1.29-Mark.1.34">Mr 1:29-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.38-Luke.4.41">Lu 4:38-41</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.29-Mark.1.34">Mr 1:29-34</reference>.<div eID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.18-Matt.8.22">Mt 8:18-22</reference>. Incidents Illustrative of Discipleship. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.9.57-Luke.9.62">Lu 9:57-62</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> The incidents here are two: in the corresponding passage of Luke they are three. Here they are introduced before the mission of the Twelve: <hi type="bold">in Luke, when our Lord was making preparation for His final journey to Jerusalem. But to conclude from this, as some good critics do (as Bengel, Ellicott, &c.) that one of these incidents at least occurred twice--</hi>which led to the mention of the others at the two different times--is too artificial. Taking them, then, as one set of occurrences, the question arises. Are they recorded by Matthew or by Luke in their proper place? Neander, Schleiermacher, and Olshausen adhere to Luke's order; while Meyer, De Wette, and Lange prefer that of Matthew. Probably the first incident is here in its right place. But as the command, in the second incident, to preach the kingdom of God, would scarcely have been given at so early a period, it is likely that it and the third incident have their true place in Luke. Taking these three incidents up here then we have,<div eID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25715" type="x-p"/> I. The Rash or Precipitate Disciple (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.19">Mt 8:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen25715" type="x-p"/>
entries.0682c9e3ed069632b786056ad411e06554ea6f9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13466"/><div sID="gen25716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13466"/>19. And a certain scribe came, and said unto him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest. <div eID="gen25716" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a5295df897ab255e9112eb5cdf81037d69c18e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13467"/><div sID="gen25717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13467"/><hi type="bold">20. And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head--</hi>Few as there were of the scribes who attached themselves to Jesus, it would appear, from his calling Him Teacher, that this one was a "disciple" in that looser sense of the word in which it is applied to the crowds who flocked after Him, with more or less conviction that His claims were well founded. But from the answer which he received we are led to infer that there was more of transient emotion--of temporary impulse--than of intelligent principle in the speech. The preaching of Christ had riveted and charmed him; his heart had swelled; his enthusiasm had been kindled; and in this state of mind he will go anywhere with Him, and feels impelled to tell Him so. "Wilt thou?" replies the Lord Jesus. "Knowest thou whom thou art pledging thyself to follow, and whither haply He may lead thee? No warm home, no downy pillow has He for thee: He has them not for Himself. The foxes are not without their holes, nor do the birds of the air lack their nests; but the Son of man has to depend on the hospitality of others, and borrow the pillow whereon He lays His head." How affecting is this reply! And yet He rejects not this man's offer, nor refuses him the liberty to follow Him. Only He will have him know what he is doing, and "count the cost." He will have him weigh well the real nature and the strength of his attachment, whether it be such as will abide in the day of trial. If so, he will be right welcome, for Christ puts none away. But it seems too plain that in this case that had not been done. And so we have called this the Rash or Precipitate Disciple.<div eID="gen25717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25718" type="x-p"/> II. The Procrastinating or Entangled Disciple (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.21">Mt 8:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen25718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25719" type="x-p"/> As this is more fully given in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.59">Lu 9:59</reference>), we must take both together. "And He said unto another of His disciples, Follow Me. But he said,"<div eID="gen25719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead--</hi>or, as more definitely in Luke, "Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God" (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.60">Lu 9:60</reference>). This disciple did not, like the former, volunteer his services, but is called by the Lord Jesus, not only to follow, but to preach Him. And he is quite willing; only he is not ready just yet. "Lord, I will; but"--"There is a difficulty in the way just now; but that once removed, I am Thine." What now is this difficulty? Was his father actually dead--lying a corpse--having only to be buried? Impossible. As it was the practice, as noticed on <reference osisRef="Luke.7.12">Lu 7:12</reference>, to bury on the day of death, it is not very likely that this disciple would have been here at all if his father had just breathed his last; nor would the Lord, if He was there, have hindered him discharging the last duties of a son to a father. No doubt it was the common case of a son having a frail or aged father, not likely to live long, whose head he thinks it his duty to see under the ground ere he goes abroad. "This aged father of mine will soon be removed; and if I might but delay till I see him decently interred, I should then be free to preach the kingdom of God wherever duty might call me." This view of the case will explain the curt reply, "Let the dead bury their dead: <hi type="bold">but go thou and preach the kingdom of God." Like all the other paradoxical sayings of our Lord, the key to it is the different senses--</hi>a higher and a lower--in which the same word "dead" is used: <hi type="bold">There are two kingdoms of God in existence upon earth; the kingdom of nature, and the kingdom of grace: To the one kingdom all the children of this world, even the most ungodly, are fully alive; to the other, only the children of light: The reigning irreligion consists not in indifference to the common humanities of social life, but to things spiritual and eternal: Fear not, therefore, that your father will in your absence be neglected, and that when he breathes his last there will not be relatives and friends ready enough to do to him the last offices of kindness. Your wish to discharge these yourself is natural, and to be allowed to do it a privilege not lightly to be foregone. But the kingdom of God lies now all neglected and needy: Its more exalted character few discern; to its paramount claims few are alive: and to "preach" it fewer still are qualified and called: But thou art: The Lord therefore hath need of thee: Leave, then, those claims of nature, high though they be, to those who are dead to the still higher claims of the kingdom of grace, which God is now erecting upon earth--</hi>Let the dead bury their dead; but go thou and preach the kingdom of God. And so have we here the genuine, but Procrastinating or Entangled Disciple.<div eID="gen25720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25721" type="x-p"/> The next case is recorded only by Luke:<div eID="gen25721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25722" type="x-p"/> III. The Irresolute or Wavering Disciple (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.61">Lu 9:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">62</reference>).<div eID="gen25722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25723" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.61">Lu 9:61</reference>:<div eID="gen25723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25724" type="x-p"/> And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell which are at home at my house.<div eID="gen25724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25725" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">Lu 9:62</reference>:<div eID="gen25725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. But for the very different replies given, we should hardly have discerned the difference between this and the second case: the one man called, indeed, and the other volunteering, as did the first; but both seemingly alike willing, and only having a difficulty in their way just at that moment. But, by help of what is said respectively to each, we perceive the great difference between the two cases. From the warning given against "looking back," it is evident that this man's discipleship was not yet thorough, his separation from the world not entire. It is not a case of going back, but of looking back; and as there is here a manifest reference to the case of "Lot's wife" (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.26">Ge 19:26</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Luke.17.32">Lu 17:32</reference>), we see that it is not actual return to the world that we have here to deal with, but a reluctance to break with it. The figure of putting one's hand to the plough and looking back is an exceedingly vivid one, and to an agricultural people most impressive. As ploughing requires an eye intent on the furrow to be made, and is marred the instant one turns about, so will they come short of salvation who prosecute the work of God with a distracted attention, a divided heart. The reference may be chiefly to ministers; but the application at least is general. As the image seems plainly to have been suggested by the case of Elijah and Elisha, a difficulty may be raised, requiring a moment's attention. When Elijah cast his mantle about Elisha, which the youth quite understood to mean appointing him his successor, he was ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen, the last pair held by himself. Leaving his oxen, he ran after the prophet, and said, "Let me, I pray thee, kiss my father and my mother, and [then] I will follow thee." Was this said in the same spirit with the same speech uttered by our disciple? Let us see. "And Elijah said unto him, Go back again: for what have I done to thee." Commentators take this to mean that Elijah had really done nothing to hinder him from going on with all his ordinary duties. But to us it seems clear that Elijah's intention was to try what manner of spirit the youth was of:--</hi>"Kiss thy father and mother? And why not? By all means, go home and stay with them; for what have I done to thee? I did but throw a mantle about thee; but what of that?" If this was his meaning, Elisha thoroughly apprehended and nobly met it. "He returned back from him, and took a yoke of oxen, and slew them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen (the wood of his ploughing implements), and gave unto the people, and they did eat: then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.19-1Kgs.19.21">1Ki 19:19-21</reference>). We know not if even his father and mother had time to be called to this hasty feast. But this much is plain, that, though in affluent circumstances, he gave up his lower calling, with all its prospects, for the higher and at that time perilous, office to which he was called. What now is the bearing of these two cases? Did Elisha do wrong in bidding them farewell with whom he was associated in his early calling? Or, if not, would this disciple have done wrong if he had done the same thing, and in the same spirit, with Elisha? Clearly not. Elisha's doing it proved that he could with safety do it; and our Lord's warning is not against bidding them farewell which were at home at his house, but against the probable fatal consequences of that step; lest the embraces of earthly relationship should prove too strong for him, and he should never return to follow Christ. Accordingly, we have called this the Irresolute or Wavering Disciple.<div eID="gen25726" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.23-Matt.8.27">Mt 8:23-27</reference>. Jesus Crossing the Sea of Galilee, Miraculously Stills a Tempest. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.4.35-Mark.4.41">Mr 4:35-41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.22-Luke.8.25">Lu 8:22-25</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25727" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.35-Mark.4.41">Mr 4:35-41</reference>.<div eID="gen25727" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.8.28-Matt.8.34">Mt 8:28-34</reference>. Jesus Heals the Gergesene Demoniacs. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">Mr 5:1-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.26-Luke.8.39">Lu 8:26-39</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25728" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">Mr 5:1-20</reference>.  <chapter eID="Matt.8"/>

entries.e90f1d97e5bd3310a86ccdaa931fe2807448db48: <div eID="gen36765" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen36766" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36767" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36767" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36766" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36768" type="x-p"/> Great multitudes follow Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.1">Mat 8:1</reference>. He heals a leper, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.2-Mat.8.4">Mat 8:2-4</reference>. Heals the centurion's servant, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.5-Mat.8.13">Mat 8:5-13</reference>. Heals Peter's wife's mother, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.14">Mat 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.15">Mat 8:15</reference>; and several other diseased persons, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.16">Mat 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.17">Mat 8:17</reference>. Departs from that place, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.18">Mat 8:18</reference>. Two persons offer to be his disciples, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.19-Mat.8.22">Mat 8:19-22</reference>. He and his disciples are overtaken with a tempest, which he miraculously stills, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.23-Mat.8.27">Mat 8:23-27</reference>. He cures demoniacs, and the demons which went out enter into a herd of swine, which, rushing into the sea, perish, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.28-Mat.8.32">Mat 8:28-32</reference>. The swine-herds announce the miracle to the Gergesenes, who request Christ to depart from their country, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.33">Mat 8:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.34">Mat 8:34</reference>. <div eID="gen36768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36769" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen36769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36770" type="x-p"/> From the mountain - That mountain on which he had delivered the preceding inimitable sermon. <div eID="gen36770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36771" type="x-p"/> Great multitudes followed him - Having been deeply impressed with the glorious doctrines which they had just heard.
entries.a6da831a18497176bff35e839b60e8ac65f57090: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen36771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36772" type="x-p"/> And, behold, there came a leper - The leprosy λεπρα, from λεπις, a scale, was an inveterate cutaneous disease, appearing in dry, thin, white scurfy scales or scabs, either on the whole body, or on some part of it, usually attended with violent itching, and often with great pain. The eastern leprosy was a distemper of the most loathsome kind, highly contagious, so as to infect garments, (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.47">Lev 13:47</reference>, etc)., and houses, (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.34">Lev 14:34</reference>, etc)., and was deemed incurable by any human means. Among the Jews, God alone was applied to for its removal; and the cure was ever attributed to his sovereign power. <div eID="gen36772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36773" type="x-p"/> The various symptoms of this dreadful disorder, which was a striking emblem of sin, may be seen in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.14">Lev 13:14</reference> :, where also may be read the legal ordinances concerning it; which, as on the one hand, they set forth how odious sin is to God, so, on the other, they represent the cleansing of our pollutions by the sacrifice and resurrection of Christ, by the sprinkling and application of his blood, and by the sanctifying and healing influences of the Holy Spirit. <div eID="gen36773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36774" type="x-p"/> The Greek name λεπρα, seems to have been given to this distemper, on account of the thin, white Scales (λεπιδες) with which the bodies of the leprous were sometimes so covered as to give them the appearance of snow, <reference osisRef="Exo.4.6">Exo 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.10">Num 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.27">2Kgs 5:27</reference>. <div eID="gen36774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36775" type="x-p"/> Herodotus, lib. 1, mentions this disorder as existing, in his time, among the Persians. He calls it λευκην, the white scab; and says, that those who were affected with it were prohibited from mingling with the other citizens; and so dreadful was this malady esteemed among them that they considered it a punishment on the person, from their great god, the sun, for some evil committed against him. Dr. Mead mentions a remarkable case of this kind which came under his own observation. "A countryman whose whole body was so miserably seized with it that his skin was shining as covered with flakes of snow, and as the furfuraceous or bran-like scales were daily rubbed off, the flesh appeared quick or raw underneath." See the doctor's Medica Sacra, chap. 2. It was probably on account of its tendency to produce this disorder, in that warm climate, that God forbade the use of swine's flesh to the Jews. Feeding on this crude aliment, in union with the intemperate use of ardent spirits, is, in all likelihood, the grand cause of the scurvy, which is so common in the British nations, and which would probably assume the form and virulence of a leprosy, were our climate as hot as that of Judea. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.4.6">Exo 4:6</reference>, and on Leviticus 13 (note) and Leviticus 14 (note). <div eID="gen36775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36776" type="x-p"/> Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean - As this leper may be considered as a fit emblem of the corruption of man by sin; so may his cure, of the redemption of the soul by Christ. A sinner, truly penitent, seeks God with a respectful faith; approaches him in the spirit of adoration; humbles himself under his mighty hand, acknowledging the greatness of his fall, and the vileness of his sin; his prayer, like that of the leper, should be humble, plain, and full of confidence in that God who can do all things, and of dependence upon his will or mercy, from which all good must be derived. It is peculiar to God that he need only will what he intends to perform. His power is his will. The ability of God to do what is necessary to be done, and his willingness to make his creatures happy, should be deeply considered by all those who approach him in prayer. The leper had no doubt of the former, but he was far from being equally satisfied in respect of the latter.
entries.ca3ea90f3397fca1ddc56e512f9dd32cefe634b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen36776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36777" type="x-p"/> Jesus put forth his hand - I will; be thou clean - The most sovereign authority is assumed in this speech of our blessed Lord - I Will: there is here no supplication of any power superior to his own; and the event proved to the fullest conviction, and by the clearest demonstration, that his authority was absolute, and his power unlimited. Be thou cleansed, καθαρισθητι; a single word is enough. <div eID="gen36777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36778" type="x-p"/> And immediately his leprosy was cleansed - What an astonishing sight! A man whose whole body was covered over with the most loathsome disease, cleansed from it in a moment of time! Was it possible for any soul to resist the evidence of this fact? This action of Christ is a representation of that invisible hand which makes itself felt by the most insensible heart; of that internal word which makes itself heard by the most deaf; and of that supreme will which works every thing according to its own counsel.
entries.15d8bbfea5493382a7960045f8e3e07cc309142b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen36778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36779" type="x-p"/> Jesus saith - See thou tell no man - Had our Lord, at this early period, fully manifested himself as the Messiah, the people in all likelihood would have proclaimed him King; this, however, refused by him, must have excited the hatred of the Jewish rulers, and the jealousy of the Roman government; and, speaking after the manner of men, his farther preachings and miracles must have been impeded. This alone seems to be the reason why he said to the leper, See thou tell no man. <div eID="gen36779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36780" type="x-p"/> Show thyself to the priest - This was to conform to the law instituted in this case, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.1">Lev 14:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen36780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36781" type="x-p"/> Offer the gift - This gift was two living, clean birds, some cedar wood, with scarlet and hyssop, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.4">Lev 14:4</reference>, which were to be brought for his cleansing; and, when clean, two he lambs, one ewe lamb, three tenth deals of flour, and one log of oil, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.10">Lev 14:10</reference>; but if the person was poor, then he was to bring one lamb, one tenth deal of flour, one log of oil and two turtle doves, or young pigeons, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.21">Lev 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.22">Lev 14:22</reference>. See the notes on Leviticus 14 (note). <div eID="gen36781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36782" type="x-p"/> Now all this was to be done for a testimony to them; to prove that this leper, who was doubtless well known in the land, had been thoroughly cleansed; and thus, in this private way, to give full proof to the priesthood that Jesus was the true Messiah. The Jewish rabbins allowed that curing the lepers should be a characteristic of the Messiah; (see Bishop Chandler's Vindication); therefore the obstinacy of the priests, etc., in rejecting Christ, was utterly inexcusable.
entries.bac13d937892b17340f0d2a56b2b1c7c3f92d89a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen36782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36783" type="x-p"/> Capernaum - See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.13">Mat 4:13</reference>. <div eID="gen36783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36784" type="x-p"/> A centurion - Εκατονταρχος. A Roman military officer who had the command of one hundred men.
entries.52a4df3f1b5d93c58744b2018c748084625f966b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen36784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36785" type="x-p"/> Lord - Rather, Sir, for so the word κυριε should always be translated when a Roman is the speaker. <div eID="gen36785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36786" type="x-p"/> Lieth at home - Βεβληται, lieth all along; intimating that the disease had reduced him to a state of the utmost impotence, through the grievous torments with which it was accompanied. <div eID="gen36786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36787" type="x-p"/> Sick of the palsy - Or paralytic. See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.24">Mat 4:24</reference>. This centurion did not act as many masters do when their servants are afflicted, have them immediately removed to an infirmary, often to a work-house; or sent home to friends or relatives, who probably either care nothing for them, or are unable to afford them any of the comforts of life. In case of a contagious disorder, it may be necessary to remove an infected person to such places as are best calculated to cure the distemper, and prevent the spread of the contagion. But, in all common cases, the servant should be considered as a child, and receive the same friendly attention. If, by a hasty, unkind, and unnecessary removal, the servant die, are not the master and mistress murderers before God?
entries.2f42e9948576e223a05a3cd22339ec2821731f43: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen36787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36788" type="x-p"/> I will come and heal him - Εγω ελθων θεραπευσω αυτον, I am coming, and will heal him. This saying is worthy of observation. Jesus did not positively say, I will came and heal him; this could not have been strictly true, because our Lord healed him without going to the house: and the issue shows that the words ought to be taken in the most literal sense: thus understood, they contained a promise which it seems none of them distinctly comprehended. Foreseeing the exercise of the centurion's faith, he promises that while he is coming, ere he arrives at the house, he will heal him, and this was literally done, <reference osisRef="Mat.8.13">Mat 8:13</reference>. There is much beauty in this passage.
entries.848592b6c7ad0fa27b0e4ffafea4a60e57f7673f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen36788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36789" type="x-p"/> But speak the word only - Or instead of ειπε λογον read ειπε λογω, speak by word or command. This reading is supported by the most extensive evidence from MSS., versions, and fathers. See here the pattern of that living faith and genuine humility which ought always to accompany the prayer of a sinner: Jesus can will away the palsy, and speak away the most grievous torments. The first degree of humility is to acknowledge the necessity of God's mercy, and our own inability to help ourselves: the second, to confess the freeness of his grace, and our own utter unworthiness. Ignorance, unbelief, and presumption will ever retard our spiritual cure.
entries.ffa688c92e709ba0762ecfa3079bd9515cc4598f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen36789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36790" type="x-p"/> For I am a man under authority - That is, under the authority of others. This verse has given considerable embarrassment to commentators and critics. I believe the paraphrase given above to be the true meaning of the evangelist. To make this matter more plain, let it be observed, that the Roman foot was divided into three grand parts, Hastati, Principes, and Triarii. Each of these grand divisions was composed of thirty manipuli or companies; and every manipulus made two centuries or companies of one hundred men. Every manipulus had two centurions; but these were very far from being equal in rank and honor, though possessing the very same office. The Triarii and Principes were esteemed the most honorable, and had their centurions elected first; and these first elected centurions took precedency of the centurions of the Hastati, who were elected last. The centurion in the text was probably one of this last order; he was under the authority of either the Principes or Triarii, and had none under him but the hundred men whom he commanded, and who appear to have been in a state of the most loving subjection to him. The argument of the centurion seems to run thus. If I, who am a person subject to the control of others, yet have some so completely subject to myself, that I can say to one, Come, and he cometh, to another, Go, and he goeth, and to my slave (τω δουλω μου) Do this, and he doeth it; how much more then canst thou accomplish whatsoever thou willest, being under no control, and having all things under thy command: He makes a proper use of his authority, who, by it, raises his mind to the contemplation of the sovereign power of God, taking occasion from it to humble himself before Him who has all power in heaven and earth, and to expect all good from him. <div eID="gen36790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36791" type="x-p"/> There are two beautiful passages in Arrian that tend much to illustrate this speech of the centurion. Καταταγεις Αγαμεμνων, λεγει μοι, πορευου προς τον Αχιλλεα, και αποσπασον την Βρισηιδα, πορευομαι. Ερχου, ερχομαι. "He who personates Agamemnon says to me, Go to Achilles, and bring hither Briseis: I go. He says, Come hither: I come." <div eID="gen36791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36792" type="x-p"/> Dissert. l. i. c. 25. p. 97. Οταν ο Θεος ειπῃ τοις φυτοις ανθειν, ανθει. Οταν ειπῃ βλαϚανειν, βλαϚανει. Οταν εκφερειν τον καρπον, εκφερει. Οταν πεπαινειν, πεπαινει. Οταν παλιν αποβαλλειν, και φυλλορροειν, και αυτα εις αυτα συνειλουμενα εφ' ησυχιας μενειν, και αναπαυεσθαι, μενει και αναπαυεται. "When God commands the plants to blossom, they bear blossoms. <div eID="gen36792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36793" type="x-p"/> When he commands them to bear seed, they bear seed. <div eID="gen36793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36794" type="x-p"/> When he commands them to bring forth fruit, they put forth their fruits. <div eID="gen36794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36795" type="x-p"/> When he commands them to ripen, they grow ripe. <div eID="gen36795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36796" type="x-p"/> When he commands them to fade, and shed their leaves, and remain inactive, involved in themselves, they thus remain, and are inactive." <div eID="gen36796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36797" type="x-p"/> Cap. 14. p. 62. See Raphelius. <div eID="gen36797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36798" type="x-p"/> This mode of speech fully marks supreme and uncontrolled power, and that power put forth by a sovereign will to effect any purpose of justice or mercy. And God said, let there be light, and there was light, is a similar expression.
entries.3ac8d5189192bc11b44e3be1d790f8c0aee992dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen36798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36799" type="x-p"/> I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel - That is, I have not found so great an instance of confidence and faith in my power, even among the Jews, as this Roman, a Gentile, has shown himself to possess. <div eID="gen36799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36800" type="x-p"/> From <reference osisRef="Luk.7.5">Luk 7:5</reference>, where it is said of this centurion, "he loved our nation, and has built us a synagogue," we may infer that this man was like the centurion mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.10.1">Act 10:1</reference>; a devout Gentile, a proselyte of the gate, one who believed in the God of Israel, without conforming to the Jewish ritual or receiving circumcision. Though the military life is one of the most improper nurses for the Christian religion, yet in all nations there have been found several instances of genuine humility, and faith in God, even in soldiers; and perhaps never more, in the British military, than at present, a.d. 1831.
entries.67ed34e6f9aebfe58f800a918f02bca64c04516b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen36800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36801" type="x-p"/> Many shall come from the east and west - Men of every description, of all countries, and of all professions; and shall sit down, that is, to meat, for this is the proper meaning of ανακλιθησονται, intimating the recumbent posture used by the easterns at their meals. The rabbins represent the blessedness of the kingdom of God under the notion of a banquet. See several proofs of this in Schoettgenius. This was spoken to soften the unreasonable prejudices of the Jews, which they entertained against the Gentiles, and to prepare them to receive their brethren of mankind into religious fellowship with themselves, under the Christian dispensation. <div eID="gen36801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36802" type="x-p"/> With Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob - In the closest communion with the most eminent followers of God. But if we desire to inherit the promises, we must be followers of them who through faith and patience enjoy them. Let us therefore imitate Abraham in his faith, Isaac in his obedience unto death, and Jacob in his hope and expectation of good things to come, amidst all the evils of this life, if we desire to reign with them.
entries.293750b8c25dba16ca668e51a5d68840c95924af: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen36802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36803" type="x-p"/> Shall be cast out into outer darkness - As the enjoyment of that salvation which Jesus Christ calls the kingdom of heaven is here represented under the notion of a nuptial festival, at which the guests sat down in a reclining posture, with the master of the feast; so the state of those who were excluded from the banquet is represented as deep darkness; because the nuptial solemnities took place at night. Hence, at those suppers, the house of reception was filled with lights called δαδες, λαμπαδες, λυκνεια, φανοι, torches, lamps, candles, and lanthorns, by Athenaeus and Plutarch: so they who were admitted to the banquet had the benefit of the light; but they who were shut out were in darkness, called here outer darkness, i.e. the darkness on the outside of the house in which the guests were; which must appear more abundantly gloomy, when compared with the profusion of light within the guest-chamber. And because they who were shut out were not only exposed to shame, but also to hunger and cold; therefore it is added, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. As these feasts are often alluded to by the evangelists, I would observe, once for all: - that they who were invited to them entered by a gate designed to receive them; whence Christ, by whom we enter into the marriage feast, compares himself to a gate, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.1">Joh 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.2">Joh 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.7">Joh 10:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.9">Joh 10:9</reference>. This gate, at the time the guests were to come, was made narrow, the wicket only being left open, and the porter standing there, that they who were not bidden to the marriage might not rush into it. Hence Christ exhorts the Jews to enter in at the strait gate, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.13">Mat 7:13</reference>, etc. When all that were invited were once come, the door was presently shut, and was not to be opened to any who came too late, and stood knocking without; so after the wise virgins had entered with the bridegroom, the gate was shut, and was not opened to the foolish virgins, who stood knocking without, <reference osisRef="Mat.25.11">Mat 25:11</reference>. And in this sense we are to understand the words of Christ, <reference osisRef="Luk.13.24">Luk 13:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.13.25">Luk 13:25</reference>. Many shall seek to enter in, but shall not be able. Why? because the master of the house hath risen up and shut to the door; they would not come to him when they might, and now the day of probation is ended, and they must be judged according to the deeds done in the body. See Whitby on the place. How many of those who are called Christians suffer the kingdom, the graces, and the salvation which they had in their hands, to be lost; while West-India negroes, American Indians, Hindoo polytheists, and atheistic Hottentots obtain salvation! An eternity of darkness, fears, and pains, for comparatively a moment of sensual gratification, how terrible the thought! What outer darkness, or το σκοτος το εξωτερον, that darkness, that which is outermost, may refer to, in eternal damnation, is hard to say: what it alludes to I have already mentioned: but as the words βρυγμος των οδοντων, gnashing or Chattering of teeth, convey the idea, not only of extreme anguish, but of extreme cold; some have imagined that the punishment of the damned consists in sudden transitions from extreme heat to extreme cold; the extremes of both I have found to produce exactly the same sensation. <div eID="gen36803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36804" type="x-p"/> Milton happily describes this in the following inimitable verses, which a man can scarcely read, even at midsummer, without shivering. <div eID="gen36804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36805" type="x-p"/> Beyond this flood a frozen continent <div eID="gen36805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36806" type="x-p"/> Lies dark and wild, heat with perpetual storms <div eID="gen36806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36807" type="x-p"/> Of whirlwind and dire hail - the parching air <div eID="gen36807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36808" type="x-p"/> Burns frore, and cold performs the effect of fire <div eID="gen36808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36809" type="x-p"/> Thither by harpy-footed furies haled, <div eID="gen36809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36810" type="x-p"/> At certain revolutions all the damn'd <div eID="gen36810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36811" type="x-p"/> Are brought; and feel by turns the bitter change <div eID="gen36811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36812" type="x-p"/> Of fierce extremes, extremes by change more fierce, <div eID="gen36812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36813" type="x-p"/> From beds of raging fire, to starve in ice, - and there to pine <div eID="gen36813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36814" type="x-p"/> Immovable, infix'd, and frozen round <div eID="gen36814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36815" type="x-p"/> Periods of time; thence hurried back to fire <div eID="gen36815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36816" type="x-p"/> Parad. Lost, book ii. line 586 <div eID="gen36816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36817" type="x-p"/> There is a passage in the Vulgate, <reference osisRef="Job.24.19">Job 24:19</reference>, that might have helped Milton to this idea. Ad nimium calorem transeat ab aquis nivium. "Let him pass to excessive heat, from waters of snow." This reading, which is found only in this form in the Vulgate, is vastly expressive. Every body knows that snow water feels colder than snow itself, even when both are of the same temperature, viz. 32, because the human body, when in contact with snow water, cools quicker than when in contact with snow. Another of our poets has given us a most terrible description of perdition on the same ground. <div eID="gen36817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36818" type="x-p"/> The once pamper'd spirit <div eID="gen36818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36819" type="x-p"/> To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside <div eID="gen36819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36820" type="x-p"/> In thrilling regions of thick-ribbed ice; <div eID="gen36820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36821" type="x-p"/> To be imprison'd in the viewless winds, <div eID="gen36821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36822" type="x-p"/> And blown with restless violence round about <div eID="gen36822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36823" type="x-p"/> This pendant world; or to be worse than worst <div eID="gen36823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36824" type="x-p"/> Of those that lawless and incertain thoughts <div eID="gen36824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36825" type="x-p"/> Imagine - <div eID="gen36825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36826" type="x-p"/> Similar to this is that dreadful description of the torments of the wicked given in the Institutes of Menu: "The wicked shall have a sensation of agony in Tamisra, or utter darkness, and in other seats of horror; in Asipatrauana, or the sword-leaved forest, and in different places of binding fast, and of rending: multifarious tortures await them: they shall be mangled by ravens and owls, and shall swallow cakes boiling hot, and shall walk over inflamed sands, and shall feel the pangs of being baked like the vessels of a potter: they shall assume the forms of beasts continually miserable, and suffer alternate afflictions from extremities of cold and heat; surrounded with terrors of various kinds. They shall have old age without resource; diseases attended with anguish; pangs of innumerable sorts, and, lastly, unconquerable death." - Institutes of Menu, chap. 12. Inst. 75-80. <div eID="gen36826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36827" type="x-p"/> In the Zend Avesta, the place of wicked spirits is termed, "The places of darkness, the germs of the thickest darkness." An uncommonly significant expression: Darkness has its birth there: there are its seeds and buds, there it vegetates everlastingly, and its eternal fruit is - darkness! <div eID="gen36827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36828" type="x-p"/> See Zend Avesta, vol. i. Vendidad sadi, Fargard. xviii. p. 412. <div eID="gen36828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36829" type="x-p"/> And is this, or, any thing as bad as this, Hell? Yes, and worse than the worst of all that has already been mentioned. Hear Christ himself. There their worm dieth not, and the fire is Not Quenched! Great God! save the reader from this damnation!
entries.9c6503d56603cf294edaaf8c5a9f70783ca99089: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen36829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36830" type="x-p"/> As thou hast believed; so be it done - Let the mercy thou requestest be equal to the faith thou hast brought to receive it by. According to thy faith be it done unto thee, is a general measure of God's dealings with mankind. To get an increase of faith is to get an increase of every grace which constitutes the mind that was in Jesus, and prepares fully for the enjoyment of the kingdom of God. God is the same in the present time which he was in ancient days; and miracles of healing may be wrought on our own bodies and souls, and on those of others, by the instrumentality of our faith. But, alas! where is faith to be found! <div eID="gen36830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36831" type="x-p"/> And his servant was healed in the selfsame hour - Εν τη ωρα εκεινη, in that very hour. Faith is never exercised in the power and goodness of God till it is needed; and, when it is exercised, God works the miracle of healing. Christ never says, Believe now for a salvation which thou now needest, and I will give it to thee in some future time. That salvation which is expected through works or sufferings must of necessity be future, as there must be time to work or suffer in; but the salvation which is by faith must be for the present moment, for this simple reason, It Is By Faith, that God may be manifested and honored; and not by works or by sufferings, lest any man should boast. To say that, though it is of faith, yet it may; and, must in many cases, be delayed, (though the person is coming in the most genuine humility, deepest contrition, and with the liveliest faith in the blood of the Lamb), is to say that there is still something necessary to be done, either on the part of the person, or on the part of God, in order to procure it; neither of which positions has any truth in it.
entries.df52e45ec937e4e81bc82535426db28b8499a714: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen36831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36832" type="x-p"/> Peter's house - That Peter lived at Capernaum, and that Christ lodged with him, is fully evident from this verse compared with <reference osisRef="Mat.17.24">Mat 17:24</reference>. <div eID="gen36832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36833" type="x-p"/> Peter's - wife's mother - Learn hence, says Theophylact, that marriage is no hinderance to virtue, since the chief of the apostles had his wife. Marriage is one of the first of Divine institutions, and is a positive command of God. He says, the state of celibacy is not Good, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.18">Gen 2:18</reference>. Those who pretend to say that the single state is more holy than the other slander their Maker, and say in effect, "We are too holy to keep the commandments of God."
entries.e0f91289df4bf7e544aca22155f3cd7452e5cdf8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen36833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36834" type="x-p"/> He touched her hand - Can any thing on this side the unlimited power of God effect such a cure with only a touch?
